subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE

speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, June 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. Allmand that Bill C-84, to amend the Criminal Code in relation to the punishment for murder and certain other serious offences, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend my remarks to be brief, probably only to reiterate the arguments that I have made in the past as a retentionist. However, whether my view prevails or that of certain other people in this chamber who are in favour of abolition does not concern me as much as the fact that we achieve a decision. I hope we will do that next Tuesday morning so that the country will know where this House of Commons stands with regard to the question of capital punishment. I would certainly resist any attempt to put off a decision for longer than that. In other words, our debate has perhaps lasted a little bit too long. It has been interspersed with so many other things that the country must wonder about the procedure of this House of Commons. I am not going to get into that.
I am not going to question the sincerity of those who believe in views directly opposite to my own on this important matter. I might question the attitude of certain members, including the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), with regard to the law for a number of years. I think people are entitled to do that. Even so, I resist that temptation and try to get myself to the main question: Are there circumstances under which one would be entitled to take away the life of another human being on this planet that we call earth? I think that such circumstances exist. I have not heard any argument that had made me really change my attitude, horrendous and barbarous as the act of taking another life may be.
A considerable amount of thought has been given to the question as to whether capital punishment in itself is a deterrent. Some years back I reached the conclusion that, in itself, it probably was not a deterrent. However, the former hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, in one of the few speeches in all of these debates that I recall, pointed out his own wartime experience and how the fear of imminent death had a great motivation for those who were undergoing the experience of war. I suspect the same
fear would exist amongst the criminal element. When I read about the hostage incidents in prisons, I say to myself that if there were some method by which the people who would dare take other people's lives so lightly could be made accountable with their own, probably there would not be as many hostage incidents in prisons.

I thank hon. members for their approval of that particular point. I realize that in many cases we are dealing with psychotic people. Many acts of murder are psychotic acts rather than deliberate and planned ones, calculated long in advance. In other words, they are impetuous acts. Apart from that, I think there is a question in the mind of the public, at least, as to the effectiveness of the punishment to be imposed. Prison terms, I suppose, could be considered a deterrent with respect to anyone who went shoplifting. Yet the amount of shoplifting in our society is extensive. Prison terms could be considered a deterrent against drunken driving, but the fact is the extent of this crime remains substantially unchanged.
[DOT] <mo)
So it seems to me one has to look to a more basic motive for the consideration of the type of punishment which is suitable. I did think that the Fulton formula of a number of years ago, the division between capital and non-capital murder, should have been given a fair run. However, it was simply repealed by the use of the recommendation for clemency. Successive governments have used this means to repeal, in effect, the will of parliament. This is what bothers me. Even if I were an abolitionist and there were a law in force, I would want the law to be carried out rather than a practice which, in effect, negates that law. This is something which has bothered me over the years-the fact that successive governments-and I do not wish to point a finger at any of them in particular-have used this technique to flout what is the undoubted will of two out of three of the people in Canada. Most of the polls bear out that figure.
I have just been talking to my hon. friend from Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. Muir). His poll was taken more recently than mine, but his figures are substantially the same. There was a survey made by the reporters of the Chronicle-Herald and here again the results were substantially the same. It seems to me that in Nova Scotia two out of three people-the proportion is actually slightly higher-think there should be some form of capital punishment. We are not a province noted for way out abberations in our thinking and I would imagine we are in the mainstream with regard to this question whether human life should be taken or not.
Capital punishment is, of course, barbarous.

speechtext:
Somebody says it is murder, but it is not murder in the sense that the victim of the person who is faced with capital punishment has been murdered. I hear an interjection from one of my seatmates; the point was being made that murder, too, is barbarous Of course it is. And capital punishment is barbarous. I suppose the slaughter of an animal in an abattoir is barbarous. When I am asked whether I would be prepared to push the lock to send somebody to death, my answer is that I am not. Nor am I prepared to cut a cow's throat in an abattoir. And I am not prepared to perform an appendectomy on anyone in this chamber, either. Those are tasks which can be set aside for others. But there are times when things have to be done whether they appear barbaric or not. So I reject that line of thinking as an argument against capital punishment.
At this point, may I put in a word for Hammurabi? I have made the argument before. It has never appeared in the press, as far as I can see, but it is not something I have invented. The Hammurabic code prescribing an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth was not the idea of a barbaric society; it was the idea of a civilized society. What Hammurabi and others who preached that code were telling us was this: if society has to extract some kind of punishment it should be an eye for an eye but not more than that; it should be a tooth for a tooth, but not a whole mouthful of teeth; it should be one person for one person, but not a thousand. It still seems to me it is a pretty good code to follow and the ordinary person in the street would be a lot happier if, after reading about the Calgary incident or the Moncton incident, or the Dartmouth incident or the sad things that have happened in Saskatchewan, he could have an idea that the people responsible, those who were so callously indifferent to the right of others to live that in some cases they even laughed when they shot down their victims, would be brought immediately to justice. If there were some minimum extraction of justice in such cases as these, he might believe there was, indeed, a strong basis of law in Canada.
Nobody is trying to be excessive, I think, in applying punishment. The trouble is we are not applying enough punishment where punishment could matter. So people, after a while, shrug their shoulders and say: Really, we are a country which does not believe in the law, or even have a law.
For these reasons I intend to continue voting as a reten-tionist and will resist any attempt to change the law in the way proposed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate on Bill C-84 goes far beyond the specific clauses and details before us. The emotions of millions of Canadians are stirred by the question of where Canada is headed- where the government is taking us. This bill to abolish capital punishment is just one further example, one of many in recent years, which places the stamp of permissiveness on Canadian society.
It is clear that no other issue in many years has moved so many Canadians to speak out, to write letters to their newspapers. Most members of this House can attest to the feelings of their constituents, for the issue of capital pun-

ishment has undoubtedly resulted in more mail to parliament than any other. The reason is that most Canadians believe this important ingredient in our system of law and order must be retained, and it is clear to them that the policy of the Trudeau government is to abolish it.
One of the most unfortunate aspects of the forthcoming division on Bill C-84 is that Canadians have been told by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that members are free to vote as they wish. There are some members on the government side who have exhibited a good deal of courage by speaking against the bill, and against the wishes of the Prime Minister, such as the member for Vancouver-Kings-way (Mrs. Holt) who, it appears, has had a good deal of practical experience in dealing with criminals. I fear, however, that her outspoken views on this and other questions will not please her party masters.
Why, then, Mr. Speaker, is this not a truly free vote? I can only surmise that if the pressures were lifted from members on the government side and strict control on the cabinet were removed, a number of Liberals would vote against the bill and in favour of capital punishment. It is becoming clear that a very small shift, perhaps even three or four members voting against the bill rather than for it, would defeat it; it is that close. This is a government bill. It is clearly not a free vote and those who say so are deceiving the Canadian people.
Canada, Mr. Speaker, is undoubtedly unique in the world when our record of violence and crime is compared to most other countries. We have escaped the ravages of war which the countries in Europe, Japan, Russia and so many others experience during the Second World War; and since then there have been wars in Korea, VietNam, the Middle East and Africa. We in Canada have been very fortunate. We have often looked at the cities of Detroit and Chicago and said crime like that could not happen here. Our cities seemed safe, and violence seen in so many places happened here only occasionally.
Well, Mr. Speaker, all that is changing. Canada will in the remaining years of this century, more than ever before, be faced with problems of lawlessness, violence and murder. Statistics clearly show the rapid growth of crime in our country. We will, I fear, be faced too with growing numbers of threats by terrorists and hijackers, all of the things which have become fact in other parts of the world. Terrorist activities are now taking place in such civilized countries as England, Holland, France and Germany. If anyone wonders about the government's concern for this happening here, let him look at the number and cost of our police and military forces being assembled for the summer Olympics in Montreal.
Mr. Speaker, the point that I am making is that if there was ever a time when we should be taking steps to strengthen our law enforcement and strengthen the support for our police forces, the time is now. We will in but a few weeks be going through one of the most critical security periods in many years in Montreal, and this is obviously clear to the government. It has drained virtually every able man from our armed forces bases everywhere. They could not cope if any serious problem arose anywhere else in our country at the same time. Just this week, support
June 17, 1976

was requested to assist in a serious forest fire in Ontario. No help was possible; our armed forces were stretched to the maximum. In spite of the tensions of the Olympic weeks and as well the visit of Her Majesty the Queen to Canada at that time, this government has chosen to attempt to abolish capital punishment in advance of that event, which can only be viewed as the height of stupidity.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) participated in this debate on Tuesday and made a melodramatic appeal to the House for the government's bill to abolish capital punishment. The Prime Minister said that he wanted to make it very clear that, if a majority of hon. members voted against abolition, some people were going to be hanged. He went on to say that 11 men are being held in Canadian prisons under sentence of death for the murder of policemen or prison officials.
I think it is fair to say that our Prime Minister has led a sheltered life. He seems to be a gentle man but a gentle man completely out of touch with the real world, and particularly with the ugly reality of today's criminal element. Our starry-eyed Prime Minister and Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) do not, I presume, recall the brutal and grisly murders of the Moncton policemen or the gunning down in cold blood of two members of the Calgary police force, Detective Boyd Davidson and Staff Sergeant Keith Harrison, so very recently. I will never forget, Mr. Speaker, the tragic picture that appeared in the Toronto Star of Pauline Maitland with her two very small and tearful children. Constable Leslie Maitland who was gunned down at point blank range and his killer is one of the 11.
The Solicitor General, the Prime Minister and his government are responsible for the present law. They argued for abolition of the death penalty but retention for the killers of policemen and prison guards. That bill was passed only 32 months ago. Since that time the federal cabinet has in every case failed to carry out that law. Canadians and members of this House were clearly deceived by the government as well; the example of lawbreaking set by the government was surely a horrible example for all Canadians.
I believe, regardless of the arguments made to the contrary, that members of parliament must have regard for the opinions of their constituents on all matters. Surely, this is the essence of our whole system. I find it impossible to ignore the fact that eight out of 10 of the citizens of Calgary South who responded to the question last year favoured capital punishment. The percentage of all Canadians who favour capital punishment is just about the same. Recent mail received in my office indicates some 98 per cent favour capital punishment for premeditated murder. Why, then, is this government attempting to impose something that an overwhelming majority of Canadians do not want? I can only believe that it is just one further example of the arrogance of this government. A truly free vote or a secret vote, and only that, would prove the sincerity of the Prime Minister's claim.
Canadians everywhere are demanding stronger law enforcement. They have seen too much of the soft attitude which places the rights and concerns of the criminal ahead of those of law-abiding citizens. They have had enough of the loose administration of justice whereby criminals, rapists, murderers and child molesters are introduced to
Capital Punishment
country club living and then let out on holidays, weekends and parole, when the safety of society seems to have been completely forgotten in our headlong rush to demonstrate our humanity for criminals, but with little concern shown for the victims of crime.
Canada has been a good place to live. Under this government we are changing that. We are not backing up our excellent police forces with rules and laws that enable them to carry out their responsibilities. Under this government the man who obeys the law and the man who works for his living is taking a back seat to the law-breaker, to those who will not work and to those who are indeed encouraged to live off the system. Added to this unfortunate ethic in our country are the government's unfortunate immigration practices.
Many arguments have been made in this debate and elsewhere that the death penalty is not a deterrent. This was the very thrust of the Prime Minister's remarks on Tuesday. I believe that common sense, which I think motivates most Canadians, will tell us that the death penalty is a deterrent. Canadians who write and speak on this issue believe that it is a deterrent. They speak on the basis of their own feelings and how they would face the threat of the death penalty. That is how I judge the deterrent value as well. There have been many examples quoted from the mouths of would-be murderers which indicate that they too have clearly planned their actions having regard to the penalty.
The government has attempted, Mr. Speaker, to "snow" the members of this House and the Canadian people by offering Bill C-83, the so-called peace and security legislation, hopefully to sneak through the abolition of capital punishment by arguing that appropriate and sufficient safeguards and deterrents exist in the package presented. The bill falls back on 25 years imprisonment; that is to be the replacement for the death penalty, and the cornerstone of the deterrence.
There are two problems with this approach. The first is that, should such sentences be carried out, they may well remove any chance of reform and rehabilitation. But, equally important, I do not believe the government will or even intends to stick with such a commitment. We may well see further legislation brought forward in the next two years to reduce substantially these terms. If there is any doubt about this possibility, I would ask why the minister has seen fit to change the present law now, when the legislation which he brought before the House and which was passed in 1973 does not expire until the end of 1977. The government urged members to support that bill at that time, when all along it had no intention whatsoever of obeying the law which provided for the death penalty for the killers of prison guards and policemen.
In 1974 there were 545 murders in Canada and in that same year six policemen were murdered. In the year 1962 to 1975, 53 policemen were murdered and, according to the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), the murder rate since 1962 has exactly doubled from 1.2 murders per 100,000 of population to 2.4 murders per 100,000 of population for 1974. The Solicitor General attempts to explain this away by saying that all violent crimes have increased by just

June 17, 1976
Capital Punishment
about the same amount. This is just what Canadians are concerned about, and if anyone thinks that patsy treatment for hardened criminals is going to deter them or protect society, he is wrong. It take force to deal with force and it takes brutal consequences to deal with brutal people.
As things stand now, an armed robber or hijacker is prone to murder because he knows he can only be given a prison sentence. He also knows, under our present system, through either parole, holidays, temporary leave, or even escape, his sojourn in custody may well be just a few years or even a few months. The risk of killing someone is truly worth it, especially if a key witness can be wiped out. We must make it clear to the potential murderer that he risks the chance of being executed for the crime. I believe that criminals value their lives as much as anyone else. Many have families and they enjoy living just as anyone else. Many would think twice before plotting murder if faced with the possibility of being hanged. The absence of capital punishment in Canada since 1961 has directly contributed to the violent crime statistics and the murder statistics cited by the Solicitor General.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said on Tuesday that restricting the availability of guns, as proposed in Bill C-83, gives every reason to believe that such measures will effectively inhibit criminal activity, whereas he suggests capital punishment offers no such assurance. Most practical people who have studied the proposed gun control law believe it is a farce, that it will force costly and unnecessary restrictions on law-abiding citizens; it will be a restriction on freedom in Canada and it will do absolutely nothing to keep weapons from those who are bent on pursuing criminal activity.
There is something I believe is known to police and prison guards as well as those who work with prison inmates but which is not known or understood by the average Canadian or member of parliament. It is that the person or persons who plot premeditated murder, terrorist killings and other t^pes of murder are not ordinary people; they cannot be treated in an ordinary way. Let us face facts. These human beings are brutal, savage and cruel people, and no ordinary rules are applicable when dealing with them.
In conclusion, I believe that capital punishment should be extended beyond the present limitations to include all those convicted of premeditated acts of murder. Persons who take the life of another while committing such crimes as child molestation, rape, air piracy, political assassination, treason and robbery, if convicted should also face the death penalty. After all levels of judicial appeal have been exhausted and no recommendation for mercy is forthcoming from the judicial process, the federal Cabinet should be prohibited from interfering with that sentence and subsequent punishment. Where a recommendation for mercy is forthcoming from the judicial process, the federal Cabinet should be permitted to commute the death sentence.
I believe, as do the large majority of Canadians, that the death penalty is a deterrent to murder, just as is any jail sentence or punishment of any kind. It is clearly a deterrent, but no amount of research will ever prove the degree. The people of this country want parliament to reaffirm that we are prepared to take a very strong stand on the

vital question of law and order in Canada. I intend to vote against this bill and thus support the retention of capital punishment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have already made known my intention to vote against Bill C-84 on second reading. Statements made in this debate, and particularly the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the House this week, make it necessary for me to clarify for my constituents who are interested, and possibly also for my colleagues, why I will be voting contrary to the expressed wishes of the Prime Minister.
Let me say first that there is no weakening of my party allegiance. If there had not been a decision to call a free vote I would have voted with the government. I do not today agree with the Prime Minister, but I would have been prepared to accept the majority opinion of my party, since my position is not a matter of conscience but of calm and very profoundly calculated reasoning.
Many speakers in this debate have made reference to the basis on which a member should cast his vote. Before I was elected to this House in 1972 I made a commitment to cast my vote on the issue of capital punishment according to the majority opinion of my constituents, if there were to be a free vote. I can tell my constituents that I would be reluctant to make such a commitment today, and since that might take a lengthy explanation I will leave that for discussion with my constituents.
A recent poll asked the question: If a member's opinion is not the same as the majority opinion of his constituents, should he vote according to his own opinion or according to that of his constituents? Of the more than 90 per cent who expressed an opinion, of the English-speaking residents, 28 per cent only said that he should vote according to his own opinion, and 72 per cent said according to that of his constituents. However, among French-language responses to the questionnaire 60 per cent said that he should vote according to his own opinion and 40 per cent according to that of his constituents. It was of great interest to me that this poll underlined another of the differences in attitude between the English and French-speaking constituents in my riding. My intention to vote against the bill is thus both a personal decision and a reflection also of the large majority opinion of my constituents.
In response to a questionnaire in my constituency, only 22 per cent voted for abolition, some 13 per cent voted for restricted use of capital punishment and an overwhelming 65 per cent voted for capital punishment for all first-degree murderers. However, my reasons may not be the same as the reasons of my constituents and it is, therefore, important that I outline the thinking that brought me to this decision.
Let me first get to the real issue and the reason I shall vote against abolition. It is certainly not because I want every murderer to hang, but it is a decision that some murderers must not be allowed to live.
The Prime Minister made four references to the consequences of our actions, and I quote:
-we will actually be deciding, when we vote on this bill... whether some human beings will live or die.
June 17, 1976

He also stated:
-if a majority of Honourable Members vote against abolition, some people are going to be hanged.
He said:
-the defeat of this bill would eventually place the hangman's noose around some person's neck.
And he said:
-those who vote against the bill.. . cannot escape their personal share of responsibility for the hangings which will take place if the bill is defeated.
The Prime Minister can be assured that we fully appreciate the seriousness of the decision we are taking. May I add on a personal note that this will not be the first time I have made a decision to participate in the killing of other persons. This applies just as equally to those who vote for abolition, for the passage of the bill. They must accept their responsibility for the consequence of their action.

speechtext:
The Prime Minister stated:
Any discussion of capital punishment must begin with the identification of its intended purpose, which is clearly the security of society, the protection of innocent people against the ultimate criminal violence . ..
It is clear that the protection of innocent people against assaults on their lives and liberty is one of the highest duties of the state.
However, it is at this point that my disagreement with the Prime Minister starts to become apparent. He says:
The question is whether state execution is an effective deterrent to murder .. . one's moral view of the justification of capital punishement is entirely-
I want to repeat here the word "entirely".
-determined by one's judgment of its deterrent effect.. . The crux of the question before us is whether execution is an effective and therefore justifiable weapon for the state to use in order to deter potential murderers.
Again, the second word I want to underline is "deter"- deter potential murderers.
Mr. Speaker, I received from the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) a detailed response to the recently expressed views of Professor Ernest van den Haag of New York University. This was an extensive response for which I thank the Solicitor General. As a result of his argument and the arguments I have listened to in the House I am not convinced that capital punishment is a deterrent. Accordingly, deterrence is not the basis for my decision. If there is a deterrent effect, so much the better. However, the arguments of the Solicitor General have certainly convinced me that there is more than a reasonable doubt of deterrent effect.
The Prime Minister goes on to say:
Our law, from its earliest beginnings, has always recognized the rights of an individual to kill another when there exist reasonable grounds for believing that killing an aggressor is necessary to the protection of one's own life or that of another.
That obviously applies in his view in the context to which the Prime Minister referred, but it applies also in police actions where a group of policemen are having a shoot-out with a bandit. It cannot be argued that every one of those police officers is using his weapon to protect his
Capital Punishment
own life. In fact, it is a calm decision which is being made that this is a means to save the life of another innocent victim be it one of the police officers themselves or some other person who may be killed as a result of this particular shoot-out.
Again quoting from the Prime Minister's statement:
. .. there are those who say execution is justified because it prevents a murderer from ever again committing the same crime. It certainly does ... But if you rely on that reasoning,...
And, Mr. Speaker, I am relying on that reasoning.
... you are killing a man, not because his death may deter others from following in his footsteps but because of what he might possibly do at some future time. To justify such a preventive execution there would have to be some reasonable grounds for believing that a convicted murderer, if released into society ... would murder again.
Again I take issue with the Prime Minister for including in his remarks "if released into society". Whether or not he is released into society is irrelevant because after all surely a prison guard or a police officer can be considered an innocent victim.
I placed on the order paper a question which clearly indicates the direction of my thinking. I should like to read this question:
For each of the last ten years, how many persons who have previously been found guilty of murder or of manslaughter after having been charged with murder, are known to have participated in the killing of another person?
If I were rewording that question today I would change the last part to read: "are known to have participated in the killing or attempted killing of another person". My thinking obviously is along the lines that innocent persons are being killed because we have made the decision to allow murderers to live. The Prime Minister goes on to say:
We know of only four people who have been found guilty of murder by a Canadian court, and convicted of murder a second time.
I suggest this is playing with statistics. It may be true in the circumstances but ifedoes not get to the basic point. How many innocent persons suffer today because of the decision to allow a person who has committed murder to live? Mr. Speaker, again I am quoting from the Prime Minister's remarks which I found to be excellent throughout except for the insertion of the few words to which I have referred previously in my remarks. He said:
My concern is for the society which adopts vengeance as an acceptable motive for its collective behaviour . . .
We will have chosen violence as a weapon against the violence we profess to abhor.
Who is so confident that he knows for sure that such an official endorsement of violence will not harden the society we were elected to improve, will not pervade gradually many different relationships in our society? Who is so confident that he knows for sure that acceptance of state violence will not lead to the greater social acceptance of lesser forms of violence among our people? Vengeance and violence damage and destroy those who adopt them, and lessen respect for the dignity and rights of others among those who condone them.
I agree wholeheartedly with the sentiments expressed in those remarks. If we are to logically follow through, then the first thing we should do would be to disarm our police forces. I can imagine the reaction of the police in this country if such a move were introduced. What I am suggesting simply, in my possibly somewhat ruthless fashion, is that personally I do not consider the lives of ten convicted murderers to be worth the life of one innocent person.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to thank you for giving me the opportunity to speak in opposition to the latest government attempt to abolish the death sentence. I find this topic a very difficult one with which to deal, as I know many members have. On the one hand, those who would have capital punishment abolished once and for all have come up with some fairly convincing data and arguments for that cause, while, on the other side of the coin, those who are in favour of retaining the ultimate punishment have also arrived at a convincing set of arguments based on a good deal of empirical evidence. In many cases, the two opposing viewpoints effectively cancel each other out. That is why we are in the midst of debate now. This is a subject that lends itself very well to polarity, and that is why the outcome never has and probably never will be totally conclusive.
After a great deal of introspection, I have taken a reten-tionist stand on this delicate issue. I asked myself questions such as: What if my son were accused of murder. Or, what would I, as a close friend or family member of a murder victim, want as justifiable punishment for the one who had committed the most degrading and unjustifiable crime of all? I am sure that these are the questions that we have all asked ourselves in preparation for this debate. Once having reached a conclusion in my own mind, based upon moral, ethical, religious and philosophical grounds, I asked my constituents for their views and opinions on this controversial issue.
It has been argued that members of parliament should disregard the views of their constituents on capital punishment and be governed entirely by their conscience. This is what the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) would have us do. That comment was made on the TV news on March 6, 1976, by the Solicitor General. I can only partially agree that members of parliament are simply representatives who are chosen to make decisions on the basis of their own common sense, knowledge and morals without consideration for the people they represent. In most cases, public sentiment demands that elected officials truly represent the feelings of the majority of citizens. Although hon. members must exercise caution and discretion when public

sentiment runs high-as with this particular legislation- they must always keep the views of the citizens in mind. A member's constituents are, after all, the ones who elected him to office. Admittedly, it is a rather difficult position when one is called upon to provide both personal leadership and public representation, but it is ludicrous to suggest that the views of the electorate should be disregarded entirely.
A random survey of my riding of Churchill in northern Manitoba has fallen in line with my expectations as to how constituents feel about this subject. Give surveys of this nature whatever credence you like, but 87 per cent indicated they did not favour the total abolition of the death penalty. This is from local survey results found in the March 28, 1976 edition of "From Parliament Hill to Churchill". This is in keeping with the rough national average. The national average varies from 80 per cent to 90 per cent, depending on the source of information. How could any member of this House who espouses the belief in responsible government and true representation of the electorate of Canada not take into consideration figures which show that people are overwhelmingly in favour of retention. Highly charged emotional reaction, you say? Or, perhaps it is a case of "herd psychology". I say, hogwash! The people of this country are fed up with a government that is insensitive to their views and needs.
The government has not had the courage to enforce the laws of the land over the last eight years. The result has been that no one, including the prospective killer, has any reason to be deterred by fear of the ultimate penalty being carried out as prescribed by previous parliaments for taking the life of another person. The House of Commons passed legislation in 1967 with provisions that any person guilty of murdering police officers or prison guards shall be subject to the death penalty. Sentences have been imposed by the courts in good faith that the law would be upheld. But each decision has, without exception, been summarily commuted. I have to say that a mockery has been made of the law. I say this because in every case the prerogative of mercy-and I hold nothing against it by itself-has been invoked automatically. No potential killer is deterred when he knows only too well that there is little or no chance that the ultimate sanction will be levied upon him.
Not only do the majority of private citizens of Canada want the law in this area restored, but many policemen and prison guards have spoken out strongly in favour of retention of the death sentence for the cold-blooded, premeditated murder of those in their profession. Even the Canadian Law Reform Commission came out strongly against sentences of life imprisonment. These individuals and associations are speaking out, and for good reason. It concerns me when those in favour of abolition of the death penalty which is to be replaced by longer prison sentences use the words "inhumane", "vicious", "barbaric" and other epithets when describing the act of capital punishment. Do those who promote total abolition ever consider what it means to lock a human being in a cage for 25 years like some animal-a term spent in agony without a glimmer of hope? They would no doubt re-examine their rationale if they seriously thought of the cruelty involved in the lengthy incarceration of a prisoner. This, to me, is a far more cruel and torturous punishment for the ruthless mur-
June 17, 1976

derer than that of quick death. Perhaps a quote from a great social critic of his time, George Bernard Shaw, is appropriate. I do not want to embarrass those to the left of me, but I could not let this relevant expert pass without some mention.
In his preface to "Major Barbara", Shaw, while speaking of the social injustice of his time, compared criminals to dogs. His often practised sardonic analogies may offend some of you. But he gets his point across through the use of this and other literary devices. In that passage, he says, in part, and I quote:
We even take the chance of their dogs' first bite. But if a dog delights to bark and bite, it goes to the lethal chamber. That seems to me sensible. To allow the dog to expiate his bite by a period of torment, and then let him loose in a much more savage condition (for the chain makes a dog savage) to bite again and expiate again, having meanwhile spent a great deal of human life and happiness in the task of chaining, feeding, and tormenting him, seems to me idiotic and superstitious.
What he is stating, in effect, is that to incarcerate a prisoner is to torment him, and to send a tormented person back into the society is to invite further trouble brought about by that torment.
We are dealing here with human lives. I think it is a far more humane punishment for a murderer of the kind of which I am speaking to receive the death sentence than it is for him to be incarcerated for 25 years. The point I am trying to get across is that we have a situation where we have a choice between the lesser of two evils: long prison sentences or capital punishment.
No utopian method of deterrence has come into practice in the Canadian penal system. Similarly, there is no sure method of rehabilitation. Leading criminologists have proven, through studies based on empirical evidence, that there is little hope for the rehabilitation of those who have been imprisoned for lengthy periods of time. Until our society advances to the stage where these problems can be dealt with in an adequate manner, the only alternative, in my mind, is the death penalty for those who have committed cold-blooded, premeditated murder or for persons whose clinically proven volatile nature makes them dangerous second-time killers.
With our modern court system and the safeguards inherent in that system, we can be assured that no one would receive the ultimate sanction unless it was proven beyond the shadow of a doubt that the accused was, indeed, guilty. This is one of the major concerns of the abolitionist, and rightfully so. But as I have just explained, this would never happen. If I thought for one minute that there was any chance guilt could be disproved after the fact, I would not have taken the stand I have.
I am of the strong conviction that it is society's responsibility to see that the murderer of the worst kind-and I described that a bit earlier-is treated in a manner according to his crime. By the same token, it is the responsibility of society to see that the family and dependants of the victim be properly compensated financially in whatever way possible. There are those who argue that to do away with a murderer does not compensate the relatives and dependants of the victim. I do not see any logical argument there. A victim's loved ones are not compensated if the murderer is incarcerated, either.
Capital Punishment
I also feel strongly that the crime rate in Canada-and that includes cold-blooded and well planned murders-is such that it calls for action by this government. I was not surprised to hear the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) say that all offences, including violent crimes, have increased substantially over the past ten years. However, on May 5 I was shocked to hear two pro-abolitionist members of this House say that Canadians perceive more violence in society than actually exists. They invited controversy-and I feel that they have received a fair amount of it-when they said that news reports and violent television shows reflecting conditions around the world tend to make Canadians feel less safe than they really are. I think this is balderdash, and it is an easy way out. That is a very shabby argument. Why do they not tell that to the families of the Moncton policemen who were brutally murdered only a short time ago? Why do they not tell that story to the family of the policeman who was killed in a hostage incident in Calgary in March of this year, the second such murder in only a matter of months, or why not to the families of the children so brutally murdered only recently in Saskatchewan? Then I would like those two hon. members to come back to this House and tell all of us how violence in our society is just a figment of our imagination.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to participate in this debate, until this week. I have been involved in a number of capital punishment debates during the time I have been a member of this House. I have reached the conclusion that at this stage in time the country desires, and has the right to expect, hon. members of this House to support the retention of capital punishment. I do not come to that conclusion with any great feeling of exhilaration. If anything, I come to that conclusion with a feeling of great disappointment because, as a long term member of this House, I could have supported abolition. Indeed, I started down that road a few years ago because I felt that we were developing a form of penology in this nation which would allow us both to protect society and produce a more humanitarian approach to crime and punishment as a result of some of the things which were happening in our society.
Unfortunately, because of things which have happened in the last decade, Canadians, by a substantial majority, have indicated a very strong belief that we can only have law and order if the death penalty is retained. Surely, if this parliament is to reflect the mood of the nation-and if members of parliament are anything, they are the reflectors of the mood of this nation-it should be indicating to the people that parliament does reflect their point of view. It is germane to the national point of view, and it should believe, as the people believe, that we can only have law and order in this nation if we retain the death penalty.
I do not think that Canadians, any more than members of parliament who believe in retention, are barbaric individuals because they feel that the punishment should fit the crime. Indeed, I believe that Canadians, by and large, would have accepted a limited form of capital punishment if the government had lived up to its commitment to the public when the temporary reform of the criminal law was presented to parliament and murder was broken down into two classes-capital murder and non-capital murder-and when it related to extra protection for law
14596

June 17, 1976
Capital Punishment
enforcement officers and penitentiary employees. But the government duped parliament and got it to support a bill which the government implemented, in effect, as total abolition when neither parliament nor the people wanted that.
As a result of that, we have done great damage to the belief that abolition could some day be achieved. You do not fool people, and you do not make people respect the law if governments do not respect it themselves. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stood in the House this week and suggested to members of parliament who will vote for retention that, by voting for retention, they will have blood on their hands because men on death row at this moment will be hanged if parliament approves the death penalty. That was nothing short of ludicrous, because if the law as it now stands had been put into effect, there would not be anyone on death row at this time. They would have met the penalty that the courts of this land, in interpreting the law, said should be the penalty. Therefore, if those individuals on death row are awaiting the carrying out of the penalty imposed by the courts, it is not the fault of this parliament; it is the fault of this government-and it is nothing short of that.
It is nothing short of ludicrous for the Prime Minister to come here and try to blackmail members of parliament who are retentionists into voting for abolition because the government has placed certain individuals in the untenable position of not knowing whether they are going to live or die. The law says they should die and the government has said they can live-at least until parliament makes up its mind whether the death penalty should be continued.
As the previous speaker, the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith) stated, nothing worse can be done to an individual than to remove hope. It is better to remove a person's life than to remove all hope of returning to society after a crime has been committed. There are people in this nation who would suggest that a criminal should be incarcerated for the rest of his natural life rather than be punished by having his life taken from him. If there is one thing that would make it completely impossible for penal systems to operate, it is to put people in institutions, without hope. Without hope, there is no way that people can operate logically in the world of today.
Lack of hope destroys everything that is human about an individual. The only way we are going to make our prisons work successfully again is by giving to those who are in them the hope of being rehabilitated and returned to society. We cannot do that with the system that exists now. That is why so many Canadians are urging members of parliament to retain the death penalty. The system as it is has not worked for at least ten years. It has not worked because there has been no driving force that eliminates the problem that puts people in the institutions in the first place.
One of the things that inspired me as a new member of parliament when I came to this House 19 years ago, and the Diefenbaker government was formed, was the approach that the Hon. E. Davie Fulton took to criminology and criminal law in general. As minister of justice, he put in place a completely new concept of penology. He broke

down the penal system into three phases. He realized that there were inmates in the institutions who were impossible to rehabilitate, and he believed there should be maximum security institutions for them. He believed that other inmates were there probably because of their environment, more than anything else, who could be rehabilitated.
Among the latter, he believed there were two classes, the young offender, the boy or girl who gets into trouble over and over again, who still needs guidance and direction in order to develop the discipline that is required to operate in society. So he suggested there should be two kinds of institutions for inmates who were capable of being rehabilitated: one, the young offenders' type of institution, and the other, a minimum security institution. The latter would be capable of handling older inmates who still had some hope of rehabilitation, but they would not be mixed with the younger inmates and perhaps teach them the kind of tricks that rehabilitation experts did not want them to learn. They knew that if they learned these tricks they would return to the institution.
Then there was a third institution, a minimum security institution that took the inmate almost back to society, but not quite. All the bars, guns and things that were associated with penal institutions in our mind were removed and inmates were allowed to operate in a daily routine that would get them back close to society. A parole system was established to assist them when they returned to society. Things were moving along in a very satisfactory manner when suddenly a group of individuals gained control of the penal operations of this nation. They came up with more kooky ideas about rehabilitation of inmates than could be imagined by anyone with any common sense. Unfortunately, many of those individuals are still in positions of influence within the Department of the Solicitor General and the Canadian Pententiary Service. The thing that disturbs me about these individuals who have all kinds of schemes about how to rehabilitate inmates is that they neglect the reason the individual is in the institution in the first place. Individuals go to penitentiaries because they cannot accept the disciplines of society. In one form or another they reject the disciplines that society demands and they break the law; in the worst form, they kill people, but they do a lot of other things as well.
When you get planners in the Canadian Penitentiary Service who want inmates in institutions to have no more discipline there than they had outside, you get a complete breakdown within the institution. We have seen it over and over again, Mr. Speaker. Ther has been riot after riot after riot, kidnapping of personnel, wanton destruction of institutions and complete failure of the rehabilitation system as it is in effect at this time. Those who are in, come out, go back in and it is a repeat performance.
When Mr. Fulton was minister of justice, the Canadian Penitentiary Service carried out an operation where discipline was the number one criterion. An inmate who went into an institution knew he was there because he had committed a crime against society. He was not there listening to apologists telling him it was not really his fault he had done something wrong, that it was society's fault and society was going to try to mend its ways so that he would be in a better position to blend into society in the future. The inmate was told that first of all he had to learn to
June 17, 1976

discipline himself, and if he showed that he could, then the Canadian Penitentiary Service would try to assist him to secure the training that would enable him to find his place in society.
That system worked, and worked well. Then suddenly we got these kooks in the Canadian Penitentiary Services who talked about the therapeutic programs they would introduce that will delve into the minds of the inmates. They were going to develop a philosophy and a psychology which would eradicate forever the criminal mind of the individual. It eradicated it very well: as I said, we have had a complete breakdown of control! Inmates are allowed to roam around the institutions, wearing anything they want to wear and as little as they want to wear. They are allowed to let their hair and their beards grow and look as dirty and despicable as possible. Nobody says a word, because they do not want to hurt their feelings.
You cannot expect to create, in the minds of inmates of institutions, the fact that they are being punished for the crime thay have committed against society if you let them operate in that way. In addition, all too often drugs are as prevalent within the institutions as they are outside. There appears to be a complete breakdown of constructive programs because there is no discipline within the institutions.

speechtext:
No, they do not say "warden" any more. Those titles are very distasteful to those who believe in the therapeutic approach to penology. You must have the right title and the right sound to the words so that you do not offend the inmates. You must not hurt their feelings, because that would be wrong, even though they are in the institution because they did something quite serious, and probably did it a number of times. The guards at the Springhill institution were told that they should not wear uniforms, that they should look like every one else in the institution. Imagine what would happen to guards without uniforms if a riot were to take place within that institution. How would you distinguish between the inmates and the guards? There would be no way. That is the degree of lunacy of some of the programs put forward by the so-called experts in penology.
The reason I talk about this is that I do not think you can separate a rehabilitation program from the death penalty. It is all part of the same package. If we can get back to sanity and produce realistic rehabilitation programs in our penal institutions, we will get farther down the road with the public as far as capital punishment is concerned.
Capital Punishment
There is little value in a government endeavouring to impose upon the public a point of view that the public does not accept. Surely, this government should know, from every semblance of evidence that is available in our nation at this time, that the public does not want the abolition of capital punishment. If the government could put in place a rehabilitation program that was workable, the public would accept abolition of the death penalty. However, until we reach that point we cannot expect the public to accept the government's view on abolition which is completely out of step with the point of view of the public. By pushing us farther down the road of abolition before the public is ready to accept it, all the government is doing is making parliament that much more of a non-essential item in the eyes of the public. If parliament does not reflect what the public thinks, then parliament is redundant.
If this House supports the abolition of capital punishment, it will be just one more nail in the coffin of this institution as far as public acceptance is concerned. If members of parliament feel that the public gets upset when we are asking for an increase in indemnity, there would be no better reason for the public taking that point of view than parliament completely ignoring the wishes of those who pay our salaries.

Surely those who pay the bill should have some say about what is done for them with the money that they pay. If this parliament ignores the opinion of more than 70 per cent of the public, it is just asking for more difficulty in the future in so far as the people of this nation are concerned.
I hope that in future the people of this nation will come to the conclusion that our system of justice can allow us to abolish capital punishment. However, we have not yet arrived at that point. We will not arrive at that point for a long time, because it will take at least a decade to undo the damage that has been done by the permissiveness and liberalism that exists within the penitentiary service at this time.
We have to reach a conclusion that is both logical and sensible within the environment that is Canada today, that is, that the death penalty should be retained, certainly for the type of heinous crimes committed in Moncton, Dartmouth, Calgary, and in the British Columbia institution. Those crimes demand that the death penalty be imposed. I can have no sympathy for two individuals who slaughtered in the way Hutchinson and Ambrose murdered in Moncton. Why should anyone in this nation have compassion for the individuals who took those two police officers out to a country spot, forced them to dig their own graves, and then killed them. They were able to resort to every protection which the law and the courts offer. But they were found guilty.
No one has asked that mercy be accorded to them, and I suggest they should now be assigned to the same fate as their victims. It would be brought about in a much more humane way than the deaths of the two officers, even though it might not be the ideal way. They should be dealt with in accordance with the sentence which was passed,

June 17, 1976
Capital Punishment
and the same principle should apply to others who have been judged by their peers to be guilty of the crime of murder, when no recommendation for mercy has been made. It is as simple as that. That is what the law demands. That is what society demands. That is what I hope parliament will say to these individuals and to others who might be considered performing the same acts as the persons who are presently on death row.
That is what the law should say. That is what the courts will say, according to the law which is on the statute books at this time. And that is what parliament should say. The people have spoken. They have said they want the death penalty retained. Parliament should confirm that the death penalty will continue to exist in this nation so long as the people desire it as the ultimate punishment for the crime of murder.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to place on record my own thoughts, in a limited time, as to why I shall vote for the retention of capital punishment in the very limited statute we now have on the books. On previous occasions I have voted for legislation which would retain capital punishment for the murder of policemen or prison guards. The alternative was the wider application of capital punishment which was prevalent in years gone by. I have been in favour of a very limited form of the application of capital punishment, mainly on the basis that sometimes mistakes were made which resulted in innocent people being put to death. However, under the present legislation the chances of this happening are extremely limited-I would say almost non-existent. With this factor in mind, I feel the limited form of capital punishment presently provided for should be retained.
I have other reasons for wishing to see the retention of capital punishment in the case of the murder of police officers or prison guards. I feel that if there is no provision for the retention of capital punishment, then police officers will often, by themselves, carry out a form of capital punishment. When the minister spoke a few days ago I took the opportunity to ask him a question, and he was kind enough to reply. He stated that he did not think police officers in this country would carry out this type of retribution. But I do not think that view is a reasonable one. In cases where a police officer is killed in what his colleagues feel is an unfair way, particularly during the commission of a violent crime, it is very easy for them to respond when the occasion arises by carrying out a form of capital punishment on their own. I think it is significant, when reading reports of violent crimes taking place, that they often contain details of the criminal having been shot to death when apprehended and that many more shots were fired than would appear to have been necessary in the apprehension of that individual.
So I think we have our choice. Do we support a very limited form of capital punishment, with a jury, with judges and, in the final analysis, the cabinet making the decision on commutation, or are we going to risk the very real possibility that capital punishment will be carried out to a certain extent by our own law officers perhaps much more often than would happen under our present laws? I feel this point has more importance than it has been credited with. We impose duties on our law officer and also dangers, but they are human beings. It would be nice to

think they always look at the law dispassionately and would not use their guns unless it were absolutely necessary. But we have to recognize the personalities of our law officers and the personalities of murderers.
There are some people in our society, no matter what one does, who will never change their ways. They only understand being hit as hard as they would like to hit. In the final analysis, criminals do have, under this legislation, the benefit of trial by a jury which decides whether or not to make a recommendation for mercy. As I understand it, juries may make a recommendation for mercy of they may decide not to make such a recommendation. Imperfect as it might be, in the final analysis the decisions of juries probably are as good a basis as any to decide these very difficult questions. With those few words, Mr. Speaker, I would like to reiterate my point of view as to the reason I shall vote for the retention of capital punishment in its limited form.
