speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can remember back in 1973 when we first debated this bill after I had been elected. It seems to me a shame this time that the government, on a free vote, one in which members are supposed to have total freedom rushing this bill through the House of Commons and trying to get it passed quickly to take away some of their embarrassment because of the fact that they are abolitionists and the majority of the country is not.
On January 26, 1973, the Solicitor General (Mr. All-mand) spoke to the measure to abolish capital punishment except in cases of the murder of police officers and prison guards. Debate on that bill did not end until October 8, 1973. Yet this time around we debated this bill on May 3 for the first time. A budget has been introduced since then, and we have a number of opposition days. The government has done a tremendous job of diffusing this debate in the country so that the people do not really know there is a very short time until the vote. Thus, I do not think we are getting the response from the public in this debate that we should. Certainly, six weeks is not, to me, long enough to have the debate before the House of Commons. I just want to put that on the record at the very beginning.
A number of the speeches that have been made on capital punishment seem to indicate that most people who are retentionists are in favour of hanging people or of disposing of them in some form or other for just about every kind of murder. As one who has done a lot of talking in the area of capital punishment, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make it very plain that the majority of the retentionists I know are only in favour of capital punishment for the most serious types of murder, that is to say, for the hardened criminals and Mafia-types who go out and kill.
So far as some of the people who are on death row right now are concerned, some of whom are from my area, I think the death penalty should be applied. First of all, there is Elery Steven Long, who killed staff sergeant Ronald McKay of the Delta police force. This was a vicious type of crime, the type for which I think the law should be carried out. There was no recommendation of mercy from the jury, and under the present law I think this man should suffer the consequences. Then there are James
June 17, 1976

Lawrence Hutchison and Richard Joseph Ambrose who killed constable Michael O'Leary and corporal Aurele Bourgeois of the Moncton police force, another grisly murder case with no recommendation of mercy. John Harvey Miller and Vincent John Cockriell killed constable Roger Pierlet of Surrey, which is adjacent to my riding, another case where I think the law that this parliament passed on the last occasion should be upheld.
I shall be talking about the speech made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) later, but I suggest that the last debate in the House on this issue in 1973 was a fraud. There was no intention by the Prime Minister to let his cabinet carry out the law that this parliament willed, and I think this is part of the problem we are facing today.
I should also like to say something about what people who are serving life sentences in jail for murder have to say about capital punishment. There was an article in the Vancouver Province of last Saturday, June 12, concerning an interview with six different murderers. I should like to quote some of the statements that they made. The first was Larry Corbett. I cannot say I have had the pleasure, but I have had the opportunity to meet this man inside jail and also to talk to one of the persons he tried to kill. He was unsuccessful in killing the woman I talked to, but he did kill her husband. I should like to quote what he said:
Given the choice between capital punishment and spending 25 years in prison as the federal government proposes, convicted murderer Larry Corbett replies unemotionally: "Drop me".
The words come out matter-of-factly. These is no doubt in his mind that after spending a quarter century behind bars, he might as well be dead.
I should also like to quote, from the same article, some of Mr. Corbett's thoughts on capital punishment as well as on spending some time in jail. He begins as follows:
It doesn't matter at this point whether you're guilty or not because they assume you are and treat you just the same. If I thought about it I'd drive myself across the road-
I think that is funny, that he would drive himself across the road.
-(to the psychiatric centre). Who wants to listen to a bleeding heart all the time?"
What bothers him most about his life sentence?
"Basically the thing that tears me up anyway, and eventually tears up most lifers especially if you're a family man, is that the longer you do, your family slides further and further away from you."
Corbett's wife and children live in the Prince George area and he sees them only a few times a year.
"Your family has certain needs and there's nothing you can do to help because you're put away. Theoretically, you're dead and you can't expect them to die just because you're in this position. Their needs and functions are the same as they've always been.
"And this is hard to accept. It's the jealousies and hurts that end up getting to you. My wife must continue functioning in a normal manner and although we've been married for 17 years, after five years in prison we're getting further and further apart. It can't help but work any other way."
Anyone who has any sense of compassion would feel sorry for an individual like this who is spending his time in jail, seeing his family only three times a year. But the one thing that the reporter did not report in this article was what the family of the murder victim has to go through. I can remember a few years ago getting a call from a lady who said that she had to see me about something very important. She would not meet me in my office,
Capital Punishment
which is where most people come to meet me, but wanted me to meet her inside her apartment building. I thought this was rather strange, so I called the RCMP and asked them to accompany me on the visit. When I got there, Mr. Speaker, I was quite surprised, as was the RCMP officer who was with me, to find another RCMP officer sitting in her apartment having tea with this lady.
She was the one whose husband was killed by Larry Corbett. He was killed in a trailer park. Apparently, this man knocked on the door of the trailer in the middle of the night; this lady answered the door, the man put a gun to her face, pushed her into the back bedroom and started to rob her. Her husband woke up, and Corbett just shot him in cold blood. Then he shot the woman and left her for dead, too. Fortunately, she managed to live, and after some months moved back into the Vancouver area. She was threatened all during this man's trial by various people, had to change her name a number of times and move from city to city to avoid some of the people who did not want to see this man convicted. That is not mentioned in the article.
I mention this, Mr. Speaker, because we all have compassion for a person who has to spend some time in jail. However, we forget too often about the victims of crime and the relatives of the victims of crime. In cases such as this, of proven, premeditated murder, people should have to pay the supreme penalty. I should like to quote further what Mr. Corbett had to say. I could go on and on because this article runs for several columns, but I just want to quote what he said about spending 25 years in jail:
"You know, normally speaking he'd never do that but now he's only going to get one chance."
He was talking about escape.
"Like, when you drop this 25 on a guy and he gets into a position where he can escape, he's not going to get another chance for years. They're going to swallow him up in one of these 'penthouses'"
Should a prisoner be successful in escaping, he becomes desperate to stay on the loose and this puts the public generally in greater danger than before, Corbett says. If he has a heavy murder term to return to, there isn't much more that can be done to him.
Inside the prisons, Corbett says, there will be a considerable buildup of tensions resulting in more jail killings and suicides.
"It takes a hell of a lot of self-discipline to walk away from a simple little thing now. But what about when you turn around and there's absolutely no hope of me getting out for 25 years. What good am I even to myself?
"Any initiative I might have is totally lost. So now rather than restraining myself I'll be more aggressive. This guy over here isn't going to restrain himself and he's going to stick it to me. So now the paranoia sets in and you figure well, okay, I've got to get him first".
One provision that is not in the bill, and which I think should be, is this. What about the man who is sentenced under this legislation and who kills a second time while inside the penitentiary? Do we just slap him on the wrist and put him in a "penthouse"? What if he kills a third time? The Solicitor General knows full well that this can happen, and probably will, under our present penitentiary system. I now want to refer to the speech of the Prime Minister the other day. As reported at page 14499 of Hansard, he said:
I want to make it very clear that, if a majority of hon. members vote against abolition, some people are going to be hanged. Their death would be a direct consequence of the negative decision made by this House on this bill.

June 17, 1976
Capital Punishment
Then on the same thought he said:
While members are free to vote as they wish, those who vote against the bill, for whatever reason, cannot escape their personal share of responsibility for the hangings which will take place if the bill is defeated.
The people of this country gave the Prime Minister a mandate in 1972 and again in 1974. In 1973 this House passed a bill that provided that people who kill policemen or prison guards were to be hanged. Yet the Prime Minister has not taken it upon his conscience to live up to that law. He is now trying to say that those who want to retain capital punishment will have these hangings around their necks. I cannot go along with that kind of logic.
The government is now proposing to institute bilingualism in air traffic control and among pilots. The Prime Minister says he is concerned about the safety factor, yet bilingualism is being forced upon these people. Will he take that personal responsibility if an airplane crashes? I do not think he will, Mr. Speaker. He also says, and I will quote him on this because I do not want to get him wrong:
Longer mandatory sentences, and the tightening of parole regulations in relation to convicted murderers will give society the assurance it needs that those who have unlawfully taken the life of another will be removed from our midst for a very long time.
I have been looking at the present situation in our penitentiaries in respect of temporary absences for murders, and I wonder if we can really take the Prime Minister seriously when he talks about removing them for a very long time. I was told on May 27, when I phoned the Solicitor General's office and spoke with Mr. Dave Tobin, that unescorted lifers are eligible for temporary absences three years before their parole date is due. That is, if the judge sets the lifer's pardon date at 20 years, he is eligible for temporary absence or day parole at the 17-year mark of his sentence, and not before. I wanted to check this out this morning to make sure I was correct, and I phoned and was told that seven years would be the earliest for unescorted temporary absence. This would mean a ten-year minimum sentence a man must serve who was sentenced to life, and he could not get one before seven years. Just before I came in here at 11 o'clock-in fact, I was here and was called out to the phone-they had phoned my office and said, "Well, we wanted to make sure Mr. Reynolds has got it right. Now we find out that they can get a temporary absence, unescorted, after only three years in jail after being sentenced to life for murder".
I wonder how secure we are going to be, with what the Prime Minister has said, when you look at some of the people who are getting out on temporary absence passes. I have the record here in response to a question I placed on the order paper. It gives the number of murderers who received unescorted temporary absences from January 1, 1974, to June 30, 1975. In that group, Mr. Speaker, there is a man, right off the bat, the first man on the list, who was convicted of murder in 1972 and has had one unescorted temporary absence. A man convicted in 1969 has had 23 unescorted absences. A man convicted in 1970, last year had 30 unescorted absences. Another man convicted in 1970 has had two unescorted absences. Another one in 1970, convicted of murder, has had eight unescorted absences. Another, in 1971, has had two. These are all individuals who were sentenced to life for murder.

There was another man convicted in 1972 who has had 17 unescorted temporary absences. Another, in 1971, has had four temporary unescorted absences. Another one, in 1970, has had one unescorted absence. Another one, in 1971, has had one unescorted temporary absence. A woman convicted of murder in 1970 has received 17 unescorted absences. Another man, convicted of murder in 1970, received 17 unescorted absences last year. There are a couple in my own area. A man convicted in 1970 received 13 temporary unescorted absences last year. Another murderer in the B.C. penitentiary received 18 unescorted absences. Another one, convicted in 1969, in Dorchester, has had 27 unescorted absences. I could go on and on, as I have pages and pages. These are murderers who have served less than seven years and are out on temporary absences, as free as can be.
That is what we are looking at when the Prime Minister tells us that people are going to be safe under this new law. It is just a bunch of boloney, and we all know it. That is why I will vote against this bill. I will vote against it for a lot of other reasons as well, but that is one of the main reasons. I cannot trust this government to make sure that the people in my constituency, which is right next to a penitentiary, will be safe. The Solicitor General knows about this, because we have had a number of escapes from that penitentiary in the last couple of years.
The Prime Minister talked about not being able to take a life without proven necessity and without proven need. I think the Prime Minister should have more faith in our courts system and in the law we have had since he has been Prime Minister. He has had a law on the books that says people shall receive the death penalty for killing policemen and prison guards. He has not lived up to that law. He has not trusted the courts and he has not trusted the jury system in this country. He should be ashamed of himself for not having lived up to the present law, and ashamed that he is forcing this bill through the House so quickly so that he does not have to look at his responsibility for the people sitting on death row in this country. The last thing the Prime Minister talked about was deterrence, and I should also like to quote him in this respect:
I don't want to hear your guesses about the deterrent value of capital punishment. I don't want to hear about gut feelings. I want proof. Not absolute proof. Not even proof beyond a reasonable doubt. A preponderance of evidence will do. A preponderance of available evidence showing that executions are likely to deter other murders would serve as an adequate justification for the act, an adequate guarantee that a human life was not being taken capriciously.
Show me the evidence that capital punishment anywhere, at anytime, has deterred other people from committing murder. My own reading of the speeches made here on this issue since the first week of May, together with the Solicitor General's daily monitoring of the debate, have indicated that no such evidence has been placed before the House.
The evidence does not exist, neither in the Canadian experience nor in the experience of any other jurisdiction. At best, the statistics are inconclusive. They prove nothing. There is no evidence proving that the use or non-use of capital punishment has had any effect whatsoever on murder rates anywhere in the world.
I would say, in response, that the Prime Minister has not really spent enough money with people who might be on the other side of the issue. I know he has got his friend, Professor Fattah, of Simon Fraser University, with whom he has spent an awful lot of money, writing on capital punishment. In fact, Mr. Fattah phoned me a couple of times to have discussions. He is a confirmed abolitionist.
June 17, 1976

Pretty well everybody the government has given money to has been a pretty strongly confirmed abolitionist.
I would suggest that the Prime Minister and the Solicitor General's department have not spent a lot of time or money with people who might be on the other side of the issue, in order to get their viewpoints and their statistics before the Canadian people. I noticed one booklet that came out, called "Deterrence and the Death Penalty", described as a critical review of the research of Isaac Ehrlich, which was funded by the Solicitor General's department, and one of the few that may have been on the other side, published in March, 1976, and done by Robert G. Hann. The author states, and he is talking about whether or not there is a deterrent effect:
However, this wisdom is replaced not with "punishment does deter crime'', but rather with "we don't know".
That is the crux of this matter. None of us really knows whether capital punishment is a deterrent. We can argue about it. I know of a case where it was a deterrent, and I am sure it would be an isolated incident and somebody might tell me of a case on the other side. We do not really know. I am wondering why this government, after having a number of years with, really, a ban on capital punishment, can say that. The government can say that it is on the books, but every murderer and every criminal knows that there is no capital punishment. Why can we not have a five-year trial with capital punishment and see how the statistics are during that time? I think this government is a little afraid to try something that the majority of the people might want. I would like to quote something the Prime Minister said a long time ago when speaking about what the majority of the people want in this country. He said:
I have never been able to accept any discipline except that which I imposed upon myself-and there was a time when I used to impose it often. For, in the art of living, or in that of loving, or of governing-it is all the same-I found it unacceptable that others should claim to know better than I what was good for me.
I find that very strange, because the Prime Minister now is saying he cannot accept things, yet he is expecting the people of this country, 80 per cent of them in favour of capital punishment, to accept his wish to abolish it. I think that is unacceptable. I have not quite finished, Mr. Speaker, so I will continue later and call it one o'clock now.
At one o'clock the House took recess.

speechtext: I thank the Prime Minister for his answer, and I apologize, through you, Mr. Speaker, for not realizing that the meeting did not start until this afternoon. However, my supplementary question to the Prime Minister is the following. The government has stated that it is committed to the reform of industrial relations. Similarly the October anti-inflation white paper invested the Canadian Labour Relations Council with the mandate of considering the appropriate avenues for this reform. Has the government had any indication prior to the meeting this afternoon that the CLC is willing to re-enter the Canadian Labour Relations Council and if the CLC is not, can the Prime Minister inform the House how his government is going to fulfil its commitment toward industrial relations reform without that very body which has been invested with fulfilling this commitment?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: METHOD OF FULFILLING COMMITMENT ON REFORM OF INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS WITHOUT PARTICIPATION OF CANADIAN LABOUR CONGRESS
speechtext:
I believe it is correct to say that there has been no firm indication by the CLC that it would want to re-enter that body, certainly not insofar as I know and I do not believe the Minister of Labour has heard that either. The reason we are meeting
(Mr. Speaker.]
with the CLC is to pursue their own desire expressed at the Quebec convention to have consultations with the government with a view to being able to play a larger role and have a larger input into the processes of government administration and policy setting. GOVERNMENT POSITION ON CANADIAN LABOUR CONGRESS MANIFESTO
speechtext: I want to thank the Prime Minister for his answer and ask him if he is prepared this afternoon to discuss with the CLC the ultimate ramifications of the CLC manifesto, which calls for a type of labour-government dialogue based on social corporatism, which, of course, is the antithesis of the past democratic practices within the CLC and the labour movement in Canada, which would be the antithesis of democracy in this country and which would make this House completely irrelevant.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON CANADIAN LABOUR CONGRESS MANIFESTO
speechtext:
I share the hon. member's concern on that score, and I imagine the New Democratic Party shares that concern, too. Certainly, our position with any group in discussions with the government, whether it be labour, management or any other sector of society, would be that the government is answerable to parliament and through parliament to the country, and not to any particular group, so to the extent that labour, or any other body, would want to have a firm hand on the decision making process, the answer would have to be no, we answer to parliament. We do not answer to any one movement.
However, of course, this does not preclude us, as we hope, from establishing ways in which the labour movement particularly could have a greater say in the input of the government in determining policies. We think it would be useful if, for example, the labour movement did not tend to be identified with any one party, but rather came as a movement representing the workers, and in so far as it did, would want to make sure the government understood the point of view of the workers.

their collective bargaining relations during this period of restraint and while the AIB is functioning.

FISHERIES
subsubtopic: ALLEGED EXTENSION OF FISHING ZONES AROUND ST. PIERRE AND MIQUELON BY FRANCE-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PROTECT CANADIAN RIGHTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister, a question which is not only important to Atlantic Canada, but indeed all of Canada since it deals with international treaties. In light of the enabling legislation covering a 200-mile limit for its territories and possessions as announced by the Republic of France, were any arrangements made by the present government to cover this contingency when phasing-out fishing agreements were signed with France? If not, what steps will now be taken to protect Canadian rights on our continental shelf which include a large part of the prolific fishing grounds on the Grand Banks of Newfoundland and which will, if not resolved, make the phasing-out agreements signed with other countries fishing within our 200 mile limit impossible to implement?

subtopic: FISHERIES
subsubtopic: ALLEGED EXTENSION OF FISHING ZONES AROUND ST. PIERRE AND MIQUELON BY FRANCE-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PROTECT CANADIAN RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should first put on the record that according to our information it is the intention of the government of France to bring in enabling legislation. Contrary to press

reports, France has not proclaimed a 200-mile limit. It is obvious that the particular situation of St. Pierre and Miquelon will cause difficulties in the boundary question which remains to be settled. This question has already been the subject of some discussion. When the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and I were in New York, we talked to the head of the French delegation. Other contacts have taken place at ICNAF. The 1972 treaty covers the fisheries reciprocal arrangement quite well. It will be a question of negotiations and discussion, as it will be with other countries where geography will not allow us to move away from each other. We share the oceans and, therefore, we will have to come to some arrangement.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding the reply just given to the House by the minister, I wish to ask him a supplementary question. What happened to these negotiations? What is the position at the moment? If France does pursue legislation to unilaterally take action on her own with respect to her boundaries, what does that do to Canada's timetable of January 1 next year?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS WITH FRANCE CONCERNING ST. PIERRE AND MIQUELON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the hon. member, who has had much more experience than I, would not expect me to answer a question starting with "if". I will simply tell him that one of the complicating factors in the negotiations with France is that of the position of France, as a member of the community and its impact on upcoming negotiations with Canada, is not yet clarified for the French themselves. I am not an international lawyer, but the possibility of having to negotiate with not one but a whole series of other countries in the community obviously complicates matters. We have underlined this problem to the French authorities.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS WITH FRANCE CONCERNING ST. PIERRE AND MIQUELON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Minister of State (Fisheries). St. Pierre and Miquelon are now claiming 20,000 square miles of continental shelf. Mr. Speaker, I think I took up about 20 minutes of my time this morning, and I hope to conclude my remarks in five or ten minutes. There are a few other points which I would like to make in this debate before concluding. One of them came to my attention this morning. I would like to mention the fact that the government has been holding back information which could have been used by all members of the House in this debate and which might have been of assistance to members in quoting statistics.

June 17, 1976
Capital Punishment
There is a booklet that came out from Statistics Canada called "Homicide Canada", of which the Solicitor General is aware. It was listed in the pink sheets which come to our offices regularly. In a debate of this type, when we are deciding such a serious question, the Solicitor General's department must have known that this booklet was being prepared for information. It was available a week ago, so it could have been made available to hon. members a month ago so that they could use the correct figures. There is good material here for both abolitionists and retentionists, and we can hope the figures are correct.
If one goes through the debate on capital punishment since the start, one finds that every member seems to have stated different figures for different types of murder, and none of the figures seem to correspond. If this material had been put in the hands of members of parliament at the start of the debate, instead of being mentioned on a pink sheet in the hope that each member would notice it, it would have been helpful to us. I think it should have been sent to every member's office with a letter from the Solicitor General's department saying that this booklet was available and should be read before the debate. It would have helped the debate come along a little further, and I think it would have made a little more sense than some of the speeches I have read. I condemn the Solicitor General's Department for making sure that that booklet was not available to the people taking part in this debate.

I do not know why the minister could not answer it on the order paper in the last couple of weeks. The Prime Minister quoted the information. There are one or two other things I would like to quote before I finish. I mentioned in my speech this morning a gentleman named Dr. Ezzat Fattah, chairman of the Simon Fraser University criminology department. I would like to quote a couple of things he said about this bill, as follows:
On February 24, 1976 the Liberal government tabled one of the most retrogressive pieces of legislation ever presented in the House of Commons-the so-called "Peace and Security Program" ...
Among the studies and programs to which the government is committing itself in the explanatory notes to C-84, one tries in vain to find anything that might allow a better understanding of the phenomenon which the bill seeks to control-the phenomenon of criminal homicide, or, put more simply, why people kill and how killing can be prevented.
And among the so-called peace and security measures one finds no mention whatsoever of any steps aimed at correcting or improving the social injustices and the social conditions that are inducive to murder.
I am happy to agree, for once at least, with Dr. Fattah and his points. I hope the Solicitor General did not use Dr. Fattah just for his abolitionist views, but also for some of his other ideas, in presenting this bill and Bill C-83. I would like to finish by talking about the committee to which this bill will go. I had intended to move some amendments at second reading to refer this bill to committee for discussion, which I thought should take place before we voted on second reading, based on some points raise by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) and by other hon. members of this House. This being a free vote, I felt that some hon. members should have a chance to discuss some of these issues before we vote on the bill in principle. But it seems that the majority of hon. members want to vote on second reading next Tuesday, and I think that is probably a good idea. Therefore, I am not going to move my motions at second reading, but I am certainly prepared to move them at committee stage and at third reading, as are other hon. members.
I just cannot see how the government can hope to get this bill through committee stage and third reading by the end of this month, and I suggest to the government House leader that the committee sessions should not be as they were on Bill C-58, and that his party should allow some government members who are retentionists to sit on that
June 17, 1976

committee. Certainly, there are some government members who are retentionists and they should be allowed to sit on the committee in relation to the number of votes. It is a free vote, and hon. members opposite who are retentionists should have the right to sit on that committee. I say that because I remember, when we were discussing Bill C-58, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) made a great speech at second reading and said she would only vote with the government on second reading to get the bill into committee where all the work would be done. Some of us who had been here a bit longer knew that that was a naive statement and that she would have a hard time achieving changes in the committee. That certainly proved true, because the government did not even allow her to sit as a voting member on that committee. She had to sit on the outside.
I suggest that the same thing will happen when the matter of capital punishment gets into the committee. The government will use its power to make sure that hon. members opposite who sit on that committee will all be abolitionists, and the bill will be hammered through committee. No witnesses will be called, a certain schedule will be set, and members will not be able to call the witnesses they want to call. On a bill as important as this one, we should have the RCMP talk to us so that we can find out their reasons for wanting capital punishment. We should hear people from the prison system. Perhaps we should hear people who have been condemned in the past, so that they can give us their views as to whether it would be a deterrent. I really do not believe the government will allow it to go that way.
Everyone wants to get out of here at the end of June. I have five children at home who would like to see me home from July 1 on, as well. When we debated this matter last time, we went right into July. I think we should have the vote on second reading on Tuesday, and I am willing to forgo putting my amendments and not to try to stall or delay this bill so that we can have the vote to find out what hon. members think about it. The government should be prepared to leave the committee hearings and third reading until the fall. I do not know what the rush is. The government has commuted present sentences-or stayed them-so it will not matter for a few extra months.

I thank the minister for his apology. I see no reason why this matter cannot go over to the fall so that we can have full committee hearings and a full debate on third reading. But the government is rushing to push this bill through by the end of June. I can guarantee hon. members that it will not get through by the end of June. There are enough speakers on this side of the House, and enough amendments which we want to discuss, so that any hon. member opposite thinking of going home on July 1 should change his vacation plans. There is no reason to believe that the government is any more honest now than it has been during the past eight years, or that the Prime Minister will allow people to be hanged. If this bill is defeated, I think the Prime Minister will continue to commute sentences, as he has for the past eight years.
I suggest to hon. members opposite that if they want to go home on July 1, their best bet is to vote against this government bill, which would leave us with the law which is in force right now: that is abolition anyway, because this government does not believe in hanging anyone. I would like to close by quoting an English philosopher, Sir James Fitzjames Stephen. He observed:
-that if murder could be prevented by the fine of one shilling it would still break the moral bonds of society to impose only one-shilling fine on murderers.
Mr. Speaker, of course, a life sentence is not a shilling- nor is it a life sentence-but to many Canadians it still seems a cut-rate price-tag on their own lives. When people feel undervalued, the moral bonds of society begin to show the strain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA
subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
that Bill C-68, to amend the Medical Care Act, be read the third time and do pass.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I shall be brief. This bill has been under consideration for a number of days on second reading and in the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs as well. The latter has considered every clause of the bill during several meetings. Further, the content of the bill has been discussed at length not only inside the House but outside as well. Essentially, the bill does not intend to reduce the total federal contribution to the cost of insured services that it pays now but rather to limit for the coming years the rate or level of growth of the medical insurance costs.
Everyone is aware that the various governments are greatly concerned about the costs increases in expenditures earmarked for health services.
Provincial governments are really aware of that and so is the federal government. On second reading and before the committee, I already had the opportunity to explain all debates preceding the introduction of this bill under study by the House, and the reasons which prompted this government to set a specific growth rate in the bill.

As a result of representations made by members of Parliament and many citizens outside the House, the government made some changes in the bill which, although they may not meet all the objectives of the opposition, will at least have shortened the gap separating us from those against the adoption of this bill. Particularly, we agreed on a formula under which the growth rate ceiling would not be established from the third year after enactment of the legislation, but determined only after consultation with the provinces through an order in council.
We also agreed that the rate would be subject to debate in the House if enough members were to ask that the order in council adopted by the government be discussed in the House. So, once again, this bill is intended to meet the general concern of the public about the rate of growth of health expenditures and, in addition, still provides for the continuation of a substantial contribution to medical insurance expenditures.
I remind hon. members that we anticipate a rate of growth of expenditures for the current year that will be 14.5 or 14.6 per cent higher than the expenditures for the previous year. Next year, that rate of growth will be 12 per cent. So I suggest that hon. members remember that since October 1975 we have asked Canadian workers to limit their demands to 8 per cent, with a possibility of adjustment up to 10 and possibly 12 per cent in certain cases in their collective agreements.
The total amount that will be available for medical insurance this year in terms of federal government contributions will increase by 14.5 per cent on a national average basis. So I think it would be wrong to suggest that the rate of increase was set too low. In fact, the discussions I had with my provincial colleagues in recent months seemed to indicate that they will be able to meet without difficulty that maximum rate of increase set in this bill, and therefore I think we will have shown the effectiveness of the legislation now before the House. I am convinced that the mere fact that it was announced in the budget of June 1975 and introduced in the House a little later in this session already had a beneficial effect as far as the reduction in the rate of growth of medical insurance expenditures is concerned.
I would also like to remind hon. members that just two days ago the government submitted to provincial governments a new financing formula that would consist in a transfer of a certain number of tax points as well as an equal per capita payment across the country. That formula met with the approval of most provinces in principle. The premiers agreed that the ministers of finance would discuss this in greater detail at their meeting early in July, and they indicated that the provincial ministers of health as well as ministers responsible for education and the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) would participate in various stages of those discussions to reach a specific and detailed proposal that would attract the general consent of the provinces and the federal government.
I am confident we shall succeed through these discussions to reach an agreement rather quickly, and I indicated that my officials and myself are willing to pursue them with the utmost speed possible. We might conclude an agreement coming into force as early as next year, if the provinces are really interested in the implementation of
June 17, 1976

such a program. But the agreement might also have to be postponed for a period of a few years in the health area, for the simple reason that as far as hospital insurance is concerned, the federal government is still committed for another four years at least. Because we must serve five years' notice, as we did last July, to terminate the agreement on hospital care.
If the provinces wish to maintain these agreements in force until 1980 in the hospital insurance area, there is nothing the federal government can do to prevent them. But in the name of the federal government, I indicated quite clearly to all provinces that if they were willing to reach an agreement on a new financing formula well before 1980, so terminating ahead of time the agreement reached under the Hospital Insurance Act, the federal government would be quite willing in turn to implement without delay a financing formula that would certainly be more flexible than the current one. It would not require the provinces to contribute an amount equal to the federal contribution. The only condition would be that the funds involved, which will be transferred in the form of fiscal points and per capita payments, be allocated entirely to the health and education areas, and meet certain general criteria such as we have in the medical insurance area. However, it is very clear we would have much more flexibility than we now have under the Hospital Insurance Act.
Therefore Bill C-68, now at the third reading stage in this House, may not be implemented for a good number of years to come. In my view it is realistic to expect that it will certainly apply this year, and probably next year also. But if we are successful, with the provinces, to show as much speed and cooperation as was experienced last Monday, I am hopeful we might have a new financing formula for health services for 1978, if not April 1977. I feel the current state of federal-provincial relations is encouraging in this area. I also feel this special bill on the limitation of medical insurance expenses will be of a transitory nature, because I am convinced that before 1980 at least we will have reached with the provinces a new agreement covering medical insurance, hospital insurance and post-secondary education expenses, to which the federal government has already been contributing for a number of years.
Mr. Speaker, this is what I wanted to say at this stage of the debate on third reading of the bill. I hope hon. members will want to consider the bill in the light of what I indicated, so that it can go through all stages without delay.

I do not think it is realistic or possible to have a system whereby some provinces continue cost-sharing on a 50-50 basis while others start having tax points and per capita grants between now and 1980. It would be difficult to do this if you had some provinces operating on a 50-50 basis and others operating on tax points and per capita grants. Mr. Speaker, that would be my understanding as far as hospital insurance is concerned. Obviously, the situation with medicare is different. It would be a matter of decision as to whether it would be worth while having a tax point and per capita system operating only for medicare while we still have hospital insurance operating on a 50-50 basis.
My own inclination would be to insist that we decide the whole issue at the same time, rather than having an ad hoc type of operation where we would be covering only part of the health field in terms of tax points. If I were to make any case, I think it would have to be on the basis of both programs being changed under a new health financing formula.

Mr. Speaker, I begin by saying that we recognize and accept the fact that there is a need for restraint in spending. I think all the provinces recognize the fact that spending in the area of health care has been going on more rapidly than perhaps they had hoped. With that in mind, we have to question very seriously the approach this government has been taking in its desire to cut costs in the health field, as indeed in any other field.
One of the important factors that has to exist in this country if confederation is to survive, and if there is to be a decent kind of relationship between the federal and provincial governments, is a feeling of mutual respect and trust between those governments. We have a situation in Canada at the present time where that feeling of mutual

June 17, 1976
Medical Care Act
respect and trust has been severely eroded by the action taken by the federal government under this bill.
Generally speaking, Canadians, and indeed people anywhere in the world, believe that if a contract is made between two parties, that agreement must be abided by both parties until one of two things happens: either the agreement expires and becomes no longer relevant for that reason, or it is renegotiated by meaningful, careful negotiation, by both parties.
A number of years ago, when the medicare law was introduced into the federal parliament, only one province-I believe it was the province of Saskatchewan- thought it could participate and, indeed, was anxious to participate in that legislation almost immediately. The remaining provinces had some very grave reservations. It meant a very substantial realignment of their own priorities. I recall reading some of the debates at that time. One question which stands out very vividly in my mind was put by one of the provincial ministers, who asked, "But how do we know that when the federal government realizes how costly this operation is going to be, it will not back out of its commitment to the provinces". We have exactly that situation now.
This reflects the fact that the Liberal government at that time was perhaps working under a good deal of ignorance. It did not think through the consequences of the legislation it was putting forward. I refer, of course, to the economic consequences. We now have a situation where the prophecy of that provincial minister is indeed coming true.
It is naive for the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) to say that the provinces now are not sufficiently motivated to try to cut costs, at least to the same extent that he is, because under the existing agreement they have maintained 50 per cent of the cost. We have a situation where one party to the contract, namely, the federal government, is trying to weasel out of its obligation to the provinces. My concern is that this kind of behaviour can do nothing but damage the relationship between the provincial governments and the federal government.
We know that costs have been rising rapidly, but we also know that taking unilateral action to change the agreement has put the federal government under a great deal of suspicion in the eyes of the provinces. If the federal government is concerned at all about its future relations with the provinces, it should reconsider this bill. Once suspicion develops in the minds of the provincial administrations with regard to proposals put forward by the federal government, it becomes virtually impossible to conduct meaningful negotiations between the two levels of government. This is the type of situation which is building up now.
I do not think I can say that we in this party are against the principle of ceilings on expenditures. What we are against is the idea that the minister can somehow make unilateral decisions and announce them to the provinces, and that the provinces can go to hell if they do not like what is offered. We are opposed to such an approach.
We recall that when the medicare legislation was first put forward by the federal government, a great deal of concern was expressed about its cost. But the federal gov-

ernment insisted that the plan should go ahead no matter what the cost might be, and to a great extent forestalled objections on financial grounds by undertaking to contribute toward the cost on a 50-50 basis. In these circumstances, the provinces went ahead with the plan, and now they are stuck with it. The Liberal government of the day devised the whole scheme. It should have known what it was getting into. Now that the picture is somewhat clearer, members across the way seem to be taking the position that a change can be made in the agreement without the concurrence of the other party.
When we first heard of this legislation, we thought it was merely a club of some sort which the federal government wanted to use to force the provinces to move more speedily insofar as the rearrangement of the cost-sharing formula was concerned. Today, however, we realize that the bill is more in the nature of a preview of what the minister would like to do in connection with all the costsharing arrangements with the provinces. I see the hon. gentleman is smiling. If he thinks I am not stating the situation accurately as far as the provincial governments are concerned, all he has to do is to think back to the beginning of this week when certain proposals were made to the provincial premiers in connection with cost-sharing.
The results of that conference were reflected in newspaper headlines of which I have one or two examples before me. Here is one from the Gazette of June 16: "Premiers talks end in uproar!" Another from the same paper, of the same date, reads: "Federal-provincial jungle is a jungle like no other." Headlines of this sort express clearly the results of the attitude the minister has taken toward the cost-sharing agreements which have been made. There is a general feeling in the provinces that the word of the government, the word of the minister, is simply no good. I hope the hon. gentleman will take the appropriate action to correct that situation. If I were in his boots, I would feel extremely uncomfortable. I suggest there will be hard times ahead for the government if it does not change its attitude. Its present course has resulted in severe damage to the contractual credibility of the Federal administration when dealing with the provinces, as well as severe damage to a variety of useful arrangements of mutual benefit. In the long run, of course, it is bound to be detrimental to confederation itself and to the people of Canada.
I urge the minister to change his mind with regard to this measure. As I say, we support the idea of restraint, but there is a factor which is more important to Canada than simply forcing this legislation through the House. If the hon. gentleman is interested in making meaningful future arrangements with the provinces, he needs to rebuild the feeling of trust and confidence which is required. The best way to begin to do this would be by withdrawing Bill C-68 and going back to the provinces with an open mind and a sincere desire to negotiate.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-68, designed to place a ceiling on the federal government's contribution to the medical care program, has been before the House for many months. Now we come to third reading. It may seem to be a waste of time to debate it further, but I think it essential that we take some time to make one last, desperate effort to persuade the government and members on the other side of the House to recognize what a dangerous course the government is pursuing with respect to the health services of this country.
This legislation is being introduced on the ground that the cost of medical care has been growing too rapidly and that therefore the government must put a cap on its expenditures in the years ahead. It is true that some minimal amendments to the bill were made when it went through the committee of the House, but the basic restrictions are still there. The mere fact that the provinces have to be consulted means very little. Consultations with the provinces in the past have merely consisted of ministers of health or the premiers being called to Ottawa to be told what the federal government is going to do, and they can either accept it or lump it.
If enough members of the House ask for a debate on whatever formula the government sets for the third year, it will simply be an exercise in futility. Members are able to express their opposition, as members on this side of the House have been doing for some months, but this will not alter the government's decision. Therefore, the fact that the government has welshed on its commitments to the provinces when they came into medicare has now become the established principle that the government proposes to follow.
The minister has been complaining recently, according to the press, about the fact that the provinces have not wholeheartedly embraced his income security program. I have attended a lot of federal provincial conferences, and I imagine that some of the premiers feel the same way that I feel about them; that is, when the federal government invites you to join in a shared program, you had better go in very carefully. Otherwise you may find that, having made commitments and set up a program, the federal government is liable to pull the rug from under you and leave you holding the baby. That is why the provinces have been hesitant about entering the income security program. They have, right here, a concrete illustration of what happens when they do go into a shared program and the government pulls the rug from under them.
This is not unusual with Liberal administrations. I remember the late 1940s, when the Hon. Paul Martin was minister of health and he induced the provinces to go into a physical fitness program. I was one of the premiers who was most enthusiastic about a physical fitness program and we set up a very excellent administration. Then three
Medical Care Act
years later the federal government walked out and left our administration with the choice either of dropping the program or financing it ourselves. The province of Saskatchewan proceeded to finance it on their own, but it taught them the lesson that when you go into a shared-cost program with the federal government, you had better have long-term commitments or you are liable to be left to pay the bill yourself.
The fact is that Bill C-68 is really the first major step in dismantling health insurance in Canada as it was originally envisaged in 1957 when the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act was passed, and in 1968 when the medicare program became nationwide. The reason is given that costs have been rising too rapidly. There is no doubt that costs have risen rapidly. However, I think the House ought to take cognizance of the fact that the cost of everything else has risen. In particular, health costs have risen in other countries which do not have health insurance, to a far greater extent than they have risen in Canada.
Those who oppose health insurance-usually those who are comfortably well off and who do not worry about meeting their health care costs-point to the United States where health care costs are met on an individual basis. In that country, as the minister has already pointed out, our American neighbours spend a higher percentage of their gross national product on health care-they have no health insurance program-than we do in Canada, where we do have a health insurance program. We have the best health insurance program in the western hemisphere; not the best in the world, but certainly the best in the western hemisphere. This does not mean, of course, that we should be satisfied to let the cost of health care continue to escalate without our doing anything to limit that escalation. All of us want to eradicate any abuse of or wastage in health insurance programs. But we ought not to fall into the trap, as some members have in the course of this debate, of laying the blame at the feet of the public for over-utilization.
First of all, only a doctor can decide whether a patient requires surgery or diagnostic procedures such as X-rays and lab tests. Any patient who walks into a doctor's office and says, "I would like an appendectomy" is not going to get an appendectomy. It is not like ordering a pair of shoes in a store. Only if a doctor decides that some care or treatment is required will a patient get it. The same is true of hospital care. A hospital is not an hotel where you check in and decide that you want a few days rest. No person can enter a hospital unless a doctor signs an admission form, and no patient can remain in a hospital once a doctor has authorized his dismissal. I have been surprised to hear some of the members of the House who belong to the medical profession-I see several of them here-advocating, in the course of this debate, the imposition of deterrent fees both for persons entering hospital and for persons who go to see a doctor.

As a matter of fact, those who take the trouble to read the report of the royal commission on health care headed by Mr. Justice Emmett Hall will find in the report that Mr. Justice Hall and his colleagues examined the situation of those provinces that had hospital insurance. They examined the case of Saskatchewan, which had rejected the idea of deterrent fees, and compared it with the provinces that had adopted deterrent fees. They found that in the province of Saskatchewan the morbidity rate and the average length of stay in hospital was less than in the provinces which had adopted deterrent fees. Therefore, in my opinion deterrent fees are not necessary.
I heard in the course of the debate some comment about hypochondriacs, people who have imaginary illnesses, taking up the doctor's time and occupying scarce beds in our hospitals. Naturally there are hypochondriacs. We have always had hypochondriacs. But there are rich hypochondriacs as well as poor hypochondriacs, and the difference is that the rich hypochondriacs are able to pay for having somebody rub their backs and keep them in hospital. The fact is that people who think they are sick, are sick. They may not be ill with the things about which they complain, but they certainly are in need of treatment, either psychiatric or counselling.

speechtext:
course we are concerned about high costs, but the answer to the high cost of health care in this country is not going to be resolved by imposing ceilings on federal government or provincial governments' contributions. In fact, I think I can show the House that the imposition of such ceilings will be counterproductive rather than beneficial.
Many years ago, when some of us were first arguing for health insurance in this country and when we managed to get legislation passed for health insurance, first in the provinces and then in the federal House, we kept pointing out that there were two phases to health insurance. The first phase was to remove the financial burden between the individuals providing health care and those receiving health care. That is an important burden, and one of the things that this country can be proud of is that we have finally removed the financial barrier, thus enabling the person who is ill to go to the doctor and get whatever treatment is necessary, and to be put in hospital to have all the benefits which modern medical science can provide.
At that time we kept pointing out that there was a second phase to health insurance. It is that if we are not going to undertake almost impossible financial burdens, we have to begin immediately to change the health delivery system. That is the problem which really faces us. What strikes me about this minister and his department is that they have known for a long time, and they have said it in some of their publications, that they way to reduce the cost of health insurance in this country is to change the delivery system and replace some of the high-cost services with low-cost services.
The minister and his department have been told this by the provinces and they have been offered the co-operation of the provinces to bring this about. In May, 1973, when the federal government proposed to the provinces that Ottawa's contribution to medicare should be equated with the gross national product, the provinces rejected that, I think in September, 1974. The provinces put forth, as an alternative, the suggestion that the federal and provincial governments should begin immediately to work on programs to replace the high-cost services with low-cost services.
As the minister admitted when he introduced this bill, the federal government agreed with the provinces to set up committees to study how this could be brought about, but in the budget of one year ago the federal government sabotaged the work of those committees. Without consultation, the government announced it was going to give the required five-year notice to terminate the hospital insur-
June 17, 1976

ance and diagnostic services program, and only a few months later introduced Bill C-68, which we are now discussing, to put a ceiling on its contribution to medicare. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) has done virtually nothing to work out with the provinces the kind of programs which would enable us to reduce our expenditures for high-cost programs by substituting low-cost programs. It is apparent to anyone that unless we introduce low-cost programs first we cannot eliminate high-cost programs.
For instance, in some parts of Canada today hospitals are being closed, but there is little value in closing active treatment hospitals if there is no place to put the patients who should be moved to low-cost nursing homes. There is no doubt that there are people in hospitals today who have suffered a stroke, who are incapacitated, and some are terminal cases-and it costs anywhere from $100 to $150 a day to keep them there-who could be cared for quite adequately in nursing homes, if we were building nursing homes. Once we build the nursing homes and can move these people into them, then it makes sense to close hospitals. But it does not make sense to close them if we have no place to put these people who are today in active treatment hospital beds.
I am sure every member of this House has come across cases of men who have had a stroke or who are bedridden and cannot be sent home because the wife is not well and there is no one to care for them. Until we get alternative programs we will not be able to cut costs. What we will do, as a matter of fact, is increase the cost in the long run, because if people cannot get into hospital and there are delays, when they get in and they are in an acute state they will stay for a long time. Everyone knows that a patient who comes in for an appendectomy may be out in a few days. If he comes in with a ruptured appendix he will be in the hospital for a considerably longer time. We are not saving money by putting the cap on. The intelligent way to deal with the problem of health care costs is to work with the province in instituting low-cost services and then be in a position to reduce the high-cost services.
The provinces have been trying to persuade the federal government to join with them in instituting cost-shared programs for such services. A lot could be done in this country by the establishment of more nursing homes, the provision of home-care treatment, meals on wheels, more extended care units in hospitals, more physiotherapy units in hospitals, more denticare programs in this country, particularly for children, in order that a preventive dental program could be carried on, and pharma-care for the aged. These are the types of programs that would reduce the incidence of illness and in the long run would cut down the cost of health insurance.
Those of us who through the years have talked about a new delivery system have been stressing the need for altering the focus on health care in this country. In the past we thought of the practice of medicine in terms of curative medicine and public health care, but many countries in the world now have switched their emphasis to preventative health programs. Some starts have been made in this country. But really there has been very little leadership from the Department of National Health and Welfare.
Medical Care Act
We have a few community health clinics which have succeeded in involving the public in programs for physical fitness, proper dieting, weight watching and periodic medical examinations with a view to curing incipient illnesses before they have reached a dangerous stage. However, these are minuscule compared to the total need in this country. We really do not have a preventative health program.
No one need tell the members of this House that in the long run it costs less to keep people well than to cut them up and patch them up after they are dangerously ill. If the government really wants to tackle the problem of the high cost of health care in Canada, we ought to be tackling the problem of preventive health programs. For instance, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) could help a great deal by offering financial incentives for doctors to go into group practice, and for the establishment of group practice in the smaller hospitals where there would be diagnostic facilities, X-ray facilities and physiotherapy units.
This would save money and it would bring about better liaison between the general practitioners and the specialists, and better liaison between the medical personnel and the para-medical personnel who operate in the health field. I believe the day must come in Canada when we will have the facilities in the various communities so that the people will go regularly to clinics, so that the health of people will be checked periodically, and so that we will have a preventative program in which we get help to the people before they have suffered serious illnesses.
What has the federal government done in this field? I am disappointed. It is now eight years since we took the first step of establishing medicare in this country. It was a forward step. The late Lester B. Pearson and his government, along with the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), who was minister of national health and welfare at that time, are to be commended for that forward step. However, we have taken few steps since to begin to change the health delivery system to any serious extent, and we are paying the price because the whole delivery system of merely curative medicine is expensive and will become increasingly expensive.
What have we done about nursing homes? Some steps have been taken, but they have been really meagre. A few communities have established home nursing care and meals on wheels programs, but only in isolated instances. Some of the hospitals have established physiotherapy units, psychotherapy units and extended care units. Many of the hospitals have not been able to do this. Such programs make a great deal of difference in the treatment of people, because outpatient units mean it is not necessary to feed and look after people in hospitals. They can come from their homes for treatment, and return again.
We have done very little to expand health clinics across this country. Many of the younger doctors would be prepared, with financial incentives, to go into health clinics across this country if they were set up. The other night I attended a meeting of health care executives. Some of the young health care personnel told me how delighted they were when they read the booklet put out by the Department of National Health and Welfare called "A New Perspective on the Health of Canadians". I do not know who wrote that booklet, but I pay tribute to whoever it is.

I must say that if I was disturbed about the government giving notice last June of its intention to terminate the agreement with respect to hospital insurance and diagnostic services, and very annoyed at Bill C-68 which puts a ceiling on the federal government's contribution to medicare, I am even more concerned about the proposals which have been placed before the first ministers this week by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
We have only fragmentary information about it. Many of the proposals are in principle and no figures are given, no base year is stated. But I take it from the reports and what the minister said today that the government is proposing that it withdraw from its commitment to pay 50 per cent of
June 17, 1976

the cost of hospital care and diagnostic services and physicians' fees, as well as its commitment to pay 50 per cent of the cost of post-secondary education. In proposing this, the government intends to replace the 50-50 share with the provinces by granting to them certain undefined tax points accompanied by equalization grants.
On the radio I heard the Prime Minister say that this will gear health costs to the annual growth in the economy, which he considers a more realistic approach to health care financing. I want briefly to give three reasons why I think this is a serious, retrograde step. First, we cannot equate health care with the growth of the gross national product. Capital costs for providing health care facilities may have to be adjusted according to the state of the economy, but health services cannot be geared to economic growth. The incidence of illness bears no relationship to our national productivity. Sick people have to be cared for and health services must be provided even in times of economic recession.
Indeed, this is one of the basic imperatives in establishing health insurance in Canada. We have no control over when epidemics may occur, and these must be dealt with regardless of the vagaries of the national economy. We can expand or contract highway construction or public building, but we cannot adjust health care to economic growth. Our first responsibility in a humane society is to get people well, and this must remain one of our major priorities. We had an illustration of this last year when the gross national product in this country showed virtually no growth, but the cost of living, the cost of health services and the cost of everything else went up. In a situation like that, how would it be possible for the provinces to provide health services which people need at a time when the gross national product stayed down? We might just as well tie the health contribution of the federal government to the temperature average for the year, or to how many gallons of water go over Niagara Falls, as tie it to the gross national product.

The second weakness in this proposal is that tax points will provide proportionately less revenue for the less affluent provinces. We are in danger of losing sight of this objective. Are we to return to the situation we once had, when the standard of
Medical Care Act

The third factor which disturbs me is that the less affluent areas of Canada will find that in order to meet their health care costs in a period of declining tax revenue, they must resort to deterrent fees and user service charges. In that event, the concept of uniform health insurance benefits will be destroyed and we shall have a patchwork of health programs across the country. The result will be that those areas of Canada which are already disadvantaged in many other respects will also have a lower standard of health care. To me, that would be the negation of the kind of Canadianism which we have been striving to create over the last quarter of a century.
In my opinion, a nation which is not prepared to make adequate health services available to all its citizens, regardless of income or residence, is a nation which is in danger of losing its vision, and when a nation loses its vision the people perish.
