speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak on Bill C-68. We have heard today considerable discussion on the philosophy of health care, especially from the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) who as premier of Saskatchewan had much to do with the development of our present form of health care. This bill, essentially, involves limiting payments to doctors from the medical care portion of the federal purse. It points up a truism pointed out by the Hon. Enoch Powell when he was minister of health in the Macmillan government in Britain when he said that no matter what happens, health care must be limited in some manner. If it is not limited by taking from patients' pocket-books, it has to be done by rationing the health care system, mainly at the doctors' offices or at the hospital door. Of course, the British national health system was limited because physicians had to see 100 or more patients within an hour or two, and people waited four or five years for elective operations which we would consider should be done within a week or two.
Probably most health care legislation is founded on the philosophy that if we spend only a certain amount of money, and if we do things right, health care will not be necessary, hospitals will not be needed and physicians would be out of a job. As a matter of fact, during the war years the British Labour party promoted the idea of national health care and told the British people that if a national health plan came into effect, hospitals would only be necessary because of lack of attention, and that with a proper health care plan hospitals would not be needed, doctors' services would be superfluous and that eventually the whole system would cost much less, and few beds would be needed. Of course, this flew in the face of reality.
Our population grows older as we keep alive those who might otherwise have died of acute illnesses such as dipth-eria and acute appendicitis. We save those who otherwise would have died of gall bladder disease, which is reasonably easily treated now, or heart conditions. These people now live longer and are hospital satistics for a longer time as they become older and more senile. Indeed, our problem
14626

June 17, 1976
Medical Care Act
is only just beginning, because our population is aging. The generation of the 1990s will be faced with a very old population. Statistics in the United States show that at the moment about four people are working for every one who is retired. By 1980, three will be working for every one who is retired, and it is expected that the figure will drop to something like 2.5 working for every one retired, assuming our retirement patterns remain the same.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands expressed the idea that yearly examinations would do much to reduce the cost of health care. That is a noble idea, but somewhat impractical. For instance, if everyone in Canada had a yearly examination lasting half an hour, assuming doctors worked an eight-hour day, those doctors would have little time left to practice the curative portion of medicine. That is just how many people there are. Of course, in the case of special examinations such as heart, brain, eye, chest or gastrointestinal tract examinations, these could go on for hours and hours. So while preventive medicine is good in itself, it takes time, and the rewards have to be balanced against this.
The ideal of community health clinics have been promoted as having the possibility of providing good health care. I can only say that very often it amounts to: Let Joe look after the work today while I take a couple of hours for golf. No matter where they work, whether by themselves, in large hospitals or in large groups, the important thing with physicians is their own reaction to their patients, and community health clinics and other health bodies have many disadvantages. In many ways they are inefficient, and many doctors are temperamentally unsuited for them. From my experience, I would say that perhaps half of our physicians should not be involved with community health centres. However, that is a personal thing.
In this discussion on reducing health care costs it seems rather incongruous that the government has reduced the portion it is spending on research by something like $5 million when we consider that we have an $8 billion-I saw that figure the other day-health budget. To my way of thinking, this is a poor method of saving money. Unless governments fund medicine, there are not many other ways to fund it. If we did not have the sort of national health scheme we have, no doubt this circumstance would still be with us. Having got what we have, however, the government of the day must provide the vast bulk of the money necessary for health research. Of course, the Cancer Society and the Heart Foundation have collected the millions of dollars across the country, but these are special cases. These two funds have a certain appeal as many people lose relatives from these afflictions.
It seems unfortunate that the minister chose this method of reducing health care costs, as it is a very difficult exercise. In hospitals, the first thing that the management wants to reduce is the drugs even though they amount only to about 2 per cent of the total budget. When you consider that other than surgery and care, drugs are the most important part of getting a patient well in any hospital, to be penny wise is to be pound foolish when it comes to drugs. But this is a feature of the modern line of thought on health care.

This bill is really superfluous now that there has been the federal-provincial conference which took place a couple of days ago when the super-parliament of Canada met; that is, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the ten provincial premiers. I doubt whether Canada can survive as a democracy in a federal system if so much of the decision-making process is to go on behind closed doors when matters of great public importance are debated.
The provisions of this bill are only one small item on the agenda of the federal scheme. While we have days to discuss the proposal in this House, the federal-provincial conference had only a couple of hours. The public and the elected members of this House still do not know what they discussed. The item referred to as the established program financing proposals-EPFP-will go a long way significantly to alter the financial structure of confederation. I am not entirely against the proposal of the Prime Minister that the provinces should now take over and administer hospital insurance and medicare, even if some inequality should exist in the provinces. There are inequalities within the present system, and I do not believe there would be many more. There would be absolutely no point in doing this if there were a de facto redistribution of constitutional power which would permit the federal government to leave the health field and move squarely into the provincial field of education, as they seem to indicate they might.
We ask what the federal government and the Prime Minister are up to. Are they trying to get out of paying for federal-provincial programs such as hospital insurance and medicare and attempting to transfer these dollars to education? The proposals to give the provinces certain tax points by which the federal government would reduce its level of income tax while enabling the provinces to raise their tax, is without meaning until it is spelled out in actual dollars and until the effect it will have on the provisions of this bill is shown.
There has been a great deal of talk about per capita grants. I have always held that it would be better, in relation to shared-cost programs, to have a system of unconditional grants which would take provincial needs into account. I realize the very great difficulty in arriving at a formula which reflects the financial structure of each province, but presumably this new system of per capita grants to the provinces would be permitted to grow with the gross national product or some other escalator.
Will this formula provide a reasonable basis on which the provinces can plan and pay for medicare and hospital insurance that will give the citizens a reasonable standard of care and with, I think one might add, some uniformity across the country? There are differences in the medical care provided in different parts of this country, which cannot be ruled out. There is no doubt that people who live in large cities have a higher level of medical care available than those who live in the country. On the other hand, people who live in the country are not so likely to be run over by motor vehicles.
I can understand why the federal government wants to get out of paying half the cost of provincially administered programs when it can neither control nor accurately predict the cost. There are, obviously, several problems. In a general way, the richer provinces like the idea of extra tax points. At least, that is my view of what came out of the
June 17, 1976

federal-provincial conference and what was voiced by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. He had a great deal of experience with this subject in his time as premier of Saskatchewan, because those were relatively hard days, although that province has now come up to the standard of the others.
There will still be problems with the poorer provinces, with their smaller tax base, being unsure that they will be able to cope with their obligations to their citizens. There will be the problem of maintaining national standards in the health care field, because under the federal proposal the tax points and per capita grants would be integrated with the actual cost of health services. As the provinces can spend the money they receive in any way they choose, almost certainly this will create some deviation in the standard of health care across the country. I do not necessarily believe this is an insurmountable problem.
In the way we measure health care, I believe there would be certain changes, but I have never been too sure that the standards we apply to health care are the best. For instance, we have hospital accreditation which, in essence, means that a group of super-civil servants go around the country looking at hospitals. The things they measure seem, to me, to reflect very little of the standard of care in any particular hospital. Teaching hospitals are rated by the American Medical Association or a branch of it which is involved in rating all hospitals on the North American continent.
Wrapped up in the proposals of the Prime Minister and their relationship to medicare financing and hospital insurance financing in relationship to this bill is the question of whether the federal government wants to get out of the funding of health costs in order that it can make a significant attack on the pattern of education in post-secondary schools across Canada. Will money that is allocated to health services such as contained in the provisions of this bill now be used for post-secondary education or in some other way such as language training or the promotion of Canadian studies?
Obviously, the government intends to introduce considerable educational content. This is typified by what came out of the federal-provincial conference a couple of days ago. There are major problems of how to relate the Prime Minister's proposals to the clauses in this bill. As I said, to me the bill seems to be quite superfluous to what we are now discussing. Here we are talking about a ceiling on hospital insurance, but in his proposals to the first ministers the Prime Minister gave no indication of how much money the federal government is talking about.
How many tax points are to be transferred? How large will the per capita grants be? With the Prime Minister failing to commit himself and making it virtually impossible for the provinces to assess the plan, it seems the height of ridiculousness when a federal official maintains that things will go much better if we can agree to the proposals first and then put the arithmetic on the proposals. Presumably, it is the federal government's idea of equality with the provinces, like the horse and the rabbit, even for the large provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
Medical Care Act
The Prime Minister in his opening statement said: "We care about democracy which entails the formation of an active and informed citizenry". When the provinces are not even informed of the arithmetic of the proposals, how can the citizenry be informed, when conferences are held behind closed doors and the government will not even reveal its figures?
The impact of this bill has been superseded by this first ministers' conference which was supposed to come up with new arrangements for the financing of health care in Canada. Indeed, the necessity of the conference began with this bill and the unilateral action to put limits on federal contributions and change the terms as legally as possible. This bill smacks uncomfortably of rule-changing in the middle of the game, a game which, incidentally, Ottawa levered most of the provinces into in the first place.
I recall in 1969 when the province of Manitoba desperately tried to introduce and modify the federal plan in order to introduce some things that would have put a brake on spending and given more flexibility to the plan. The federal government was adamant; it was "all or nothing." The minister of health for Ontario, Mr. Miller, said what the Prime Minister had done was the most infamous action since the bombing of Pearl Harbour.
This bill has set the stage for the opting out of all provinces from the shared-cost program. It certainly is interesting to see the reaction of the provinces when faced with this. The proposition that the Prime Minister put forward to the conference, and which is embodied in this bill-"it is not the money, it is the principle"-did not turn out to be a very satisfactory one for the first ministers' conference on dominion-provincial fiscal arrangements.
Quebec, which had taken its tax points and which had perhaps foreseen that the federal government would opt out of the arrangements that the Pearson administration had set up, could have afforded to take the view that it could face the issue with equanimity. There was no answer to questions such as, "What proportion of the transfer will be in tax points?" or, "What will the equalization basis be and what proportion will be in cash?" The province of Quebec talked about the principle of keeping the federal finger out of the education pie. The maritimes obviously talked about the formula being deleterious for the poorer provinces, while Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia talked about the principle being good for richer provinces, and they all joined in the chorus of the federal government's reneging on earlier revenue guarantees.
There was even the odd one who had some thoughts about principle, that is, whether or not Ottawa, by backing out of fiscal and administrative responsibility, would be weakening the Canadian capacity to have national social standards in the national economic interest. As this bill indicates, the opting out formula which Quebec had from the very beginning is obviously the one that all provinces should have. The opting out formula that was to recognize Quebec's special status as the homeland of the French Canadian community seems now to be extended to other provinces as well.
We have to recognize that even in the opting out formula, which is essentially what the government has proposed, there will be more autonomy in different regions and provinces. This will create new standards and new

June 17, 1976

difficulties. It may well be a more divisive force in the country than we see at the present time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to say a few words on the bill before us. It is perhaps largely because of my Saskatchewan background that I am concerned about the situation with regard to the medical profession in this country, hospitals, medicare and the like. When the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) was premier of my province, he and his government introduced the first hospitalization plan in the history of, not just Canada but North America. That was quite a feat for a very small, at that time, rural province which did not have much of a base outside the grain and agricultural economy, an economy subject to the whims of not just the international grain situation but the weather at home, an economy which was then in the stages of being developed. That was done without the aid of federal financing. It was done without the support of the federal government. I believe that was in 1946.
That was followed by the introduction in Saskatchewan of medicare in the early sixties. Again, it was a first in the history of, not only Canada but North America. I remember that time very well. I was still in high school when medicare was brought in. There was a vicious fight

in my province because of the strike of the medical profession in Saskatchewan. They were calling it state medicine, socialist medicine, an infringement upon the freedom of doctors, an infringement upon the freedom of an individual to see his doctor, and so on. That was a battle that was hard fought. It was a battle that was won. From there we have seen the growth of medical services and facilities all across this country.
A few years ago the federal government took the position of supporting hospitalization and medicare by doing a lot of the funding of these programs all across this country. There was a federal Liberal government which I thought was moving in a very progressive direction, putting more and more funds into what in fact in the most important thing in life, the health of Canadians. They were moving in a very progressive direction, getting more and more involved and participating more. Then all of a sudden we have this bill brought before us today for third and final reading, a bill which I am convinced, if it passes third reading, will allow the government to withdraw more and more from the financing of hospitalization and medicare in this country. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that if this were allowed to happen it would be a highly retrograde step, something which should not take place if we think of the future of Canadians and generations to come. Should the bill pass through the House it will result in great hardship falling on many Canadians, particularly those in the have-not provinces.
Back in 1968 the government said a great deal about regional disparities. It talked about a "Just Society . It is readily seen that a large part of a just society is making sure that medical plans and medical facilities are available to any Canadian no matter where he or she may live; that there is equal access to those facilities, regardless of the income or background of that person. It this bill goes through and if the federal government withdraws from some of the commitments it has made in terms of financing medicine across the country, the time will shortly come when many of the provinces-the Atlantic provinces, for example, which are much worse off than most of the rest of Canada-will be obliged to lower their standards of care and treatment. I think of the Atlantic provinces not being able to expand their medical facilities, not being able to purchase as much of the new and modern equipment, and therefore being able to offer only a lower standard of medical services and facilities to their people. I do not think that is fair, Mr. Speaker. The federal government should be involved in medical care throughout this country if there is to be uniformity of service in all parts of Canada.
As the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie) said, it may be very attractive for some of the wealthier provinces like Ontario, Alberta and perhaps, British Columbia, to have additional taxation points when it comes to funding things like medicare, hospitals, etc., but it is not so attractive to poor provinces like Newfoundland, because the taxation base they have is so much smaller than that in the province of Ontario or British Columbia or Alberta. If the federal government withdraws, we shall see a pattern of diminishing services occurring in those poorer provinces.
June 17, 1976

We shall likely see in the not too distant future, the imposition of deterrent fees, utilization fees or user fees- whatever name you wish to use-in the provinces as one of the ways to help pay for medical facilities. In Saskatchewan we have the experience of deterrent fees. I remember very well a Liberal government in my province, back in the late sixties, imposing what it called a deterrent fee. If you went to a doctor's office you had to pay something like $2.50 per visit, regardless of the reason for your visit. When entering hospital you had to pay a utilization fee, no matter how long your stay or for what reason you entered the hospital. I do not think that is fair because these fees are nothing short of an extra tax upon those who are sick. I believe medical services and the availability of medical facilities must be universal regardless of where Canadians live.
If you are in Alberta, where they have all the oil money, or in the province of Ontario, with its wealthy industrial base, there would not be any need for a government with any social conscience to impose a deterrent fee of any kind. They could probably expand in the area of hospital care. But really, what choice is open to Newfoundland, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia or Prince Edward Island? Indeed the same thing applies if you are in Saskatchewan or Manitoba and the farm economy happens to go into a downhill slide, as it did back in 1969-70 and you lose the potential taxation base.
It is true things are good right now in Saskatchewan. They are good in Manitoba. But that is because we now get a higher price for the grain we are selling on the international market. The hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) knows that. He is just taking his seat. He recalls the policies of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) who is responsible for the Wheat Board. Back a few years ago we got just $1.97 for our grain. I am sure he remembers that. The minister was paying people not to grow wheat. The economy of the prairies was in bad, bad shape. And at that time had the federal government withdrawn financing from hospitals, medicare, and so on, we would have had no choice in our province but to increase drastically the taxation of the people of Saskatchewan or cut back on the services and facilities available.
I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the cycle in agriculture which has been evident throughout man's history is probably going to continue. The time could well come when we would not have the base in the province of Saskatchewan or in Manitoba to finance the facilities which we enjoy today and this in spite of the fact that we are expanding, that we do have excellent governments, and that our provinces are diversifying their economies.
Another point I would like to mention, is that the federal government should be getting more involved in all aspects of medicine, not just in terms of what we are doing today, but in the future. We should be putting a great deal more emphasis on preventive medicine-finding out why people go to hospitals and helping before they get ill.
About a year ago the Food Prices Review Board commissioned a study on nutrition in Canada. One of the results published in that report-something which really astounded me-was that occupancy of about 40 per cent of the hospital beds in this country may be linked to improper or inadequate nutrition amongst Canadians. I believe it was
Medical Care Act
also said that if you were to eliminate this cause of ill-health you would probably save about $2 billion in one year in hospitalization costs alone. If we had a proper food policy in this country we would not only improve the health of Canadians but we could bring down the cost of medicare and hospitalization in a very real way. Why do we not institute innovative programs to teach our citizens about good nutrition?
The same report said that about 70 per cent of old age pensioners in this country were suffering from calcium deficiency. Despite that, farmers have been told to cut back on their production of milk-that we have too much milk and production must be cut back by 16 or 18 per cent. They are told to suffer a drop in income. There is calcium in milk and there are people suffering from calcium deficiency. It would be possible to organize a school milk program; we could place a subsidy of fluid milk, and on milk products in order that people might buy more, be healthier, and eat more nutritious foods. This would be a beneficial, long-term investment, strictly in dollars and cents terms, let alone what it would mean in terms of people, of human beings who live in our country.
I visit schools. I believe the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski) does this once in a while. I went to a school last week in his riding. I see in the schools coke machines and pop machines, and kids drinking the Coke and the Pepsi, but I do not see many milk machines in the schools, Mr. Speaker. I ask why, when we in this country produce a surplus of milk, we do not have a school milk program through which students can have milk every day in the schools, free of charge?

speechtext:
I commend them on their action. I believe all provincial governments should follow their example. But a lot could be done by the federal government. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) was asked about a school milk program a week or so ago. He said he would ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) to look into the matter. I would like to see the minister take the lead in this field by calling the provincial governments together and saying, "Look, we are willing to help you finance a school milk program in a serious way." I do not know exactly how it would be set up. Perhaps it would be on a 50-50 basis. Perhaps it would be on a 60-40 basis. Maybe the federal government could supply the milk and the provinces could set up a delivery system.
We have the capacity to produce milk in this country yet we are asking people to cut back the production of milk when there are people who are suffering as a result of an inadequate diet. People around the world are starving, yet the government tells farmers not to produce more milk. It is no wonder that they come to Ottawa and throw cheese and powdered milk at the Minister of Agriculture. When farmers can produce food it is immoral to tell them not to do so. This milk could be used in our own schools, rather

June 17, 1976
Medical Care Act
than have our children drink coke and other liquids that are not nearly so nutritious as milk.
Another matter that I think the government should treat much more seriously is additional money for medical research. As a result of research we may find cures for a lot of diseases that are presently plaguing Canadians. I talk not only of finding a cure for cancer and heart disease but of a number of other diseases afflicting Canadians. I think of people in my own family suffering from rheumatoid arthritis. These people have to go through life taking painkillers because no medicine has yet been discovered to cure diseases of that kind. Yet the government is cutting back on money that should be spent on medical research, and I think that that is a crime and a shame.
I realize that we need restraint in various parts of the economy, but surely to God there are certain areas of the economy that should not be controlled, and I suggest one of them is medical research. I hope that the majority of the members of this House feel the same way.
It seems to me that all too often things are not done unless it is profitable to do them. Let me give one example of research that is being done in the food industry. In the United States they found out that a lot of the protein in chicken food went into the feathers. So a few guys had the bright idea of breeding, through genetic engineering, a featherless chicken, and then the protein, instead of going into the feathers, would go into the chicken and you would make more money with fewer chickens. A featherless chicken has in fact been bred in the United States, but unfortunately it suffered from a number of side-effects such as pneumonia, nervous conditions, and probably sunburn. My point is that you do not do this kind of thing unless it is profitable.
They have also discovered that when people buy chicken, whether Kentucky fried chicken or other kinds, they prefer the drumsticks, and they are now in the process of trying to breed a chicken that has four legs-the fourlegged chicken. You do not do that unless it is profitable.

Before I take my seat let me say we should be more concerned about uniformity of health plans and programs. You will not get uniformity if the government begins to pull out of some of its commitments. You cannot get equity or equality in this way. As a socialist I believe that it is not enough in this country to talk about equality of opportunity, about laws, peace and understanding, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) does. I think what we have to talk about is equality of conditions for all Canadians, regardless of where they live or what their backgrounds may be, be they in oil rich Alberta or in a province like Newfoundland.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether I am forewarned or what the situation is, but before I get to the meat of my remarks I should like to share with the House a few observations that I have made during the course of my brief stay here of two years. It has not been prevalent in this debate because I think hon. members have treated the subject matter very responsibly, but when I go back to the debate on the motion moved on our opposition day which condemned the government for its failure to act in regard to medical research, all members on all sides of the House were guilty of playing politics. We saw hon. members opposite condemning the Conservatives when our critic had to go to the graduation ceremonies of his daughter; and we saw members on this side condemning the government when, for legitimate reasons, the minister and his parliamentary secretary had to be absent from the House. However, in all fairness it should be pointed out that the minister's capable parliamentary secretary has been here for the majority of this debate.
If one also goes back to the budget debate one can see the cross-play that took place. The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) spent pratically all his time criticizing what our critic, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), said in his participation in the budget debate. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) devoted half his speech to criticizing the proposals that we had put forward. I had always thought that this was the role of the opposition. It may be that the Prime Minister is indulging in the role of the opposition because he is preparing himself for that role in the future.

June 17, 1976

The bill before the House proposes to limit government spending on health care costs. The only way that we can realistically hope to accomplish a cutback in this area is to be realistic about our expenditures on medical research. The hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) did an excellent job of conveying that to the House. I also have a few thoughts that I wish to share in that particular area.
On May 28 the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs was told a story, a horror story, and unfortunately it is a true story. It is called "The Slaughter in Tunney's Pasture, 1976" and it was told by Dr. Kaplan, chairman of the Canadian Federation of Biological Societies. The slaughter is brought about by the amputation of an anticipated $5 million from the federal budget for the Medical Research Council, leaving it slightly over $50 million. In terms of real dollars this means a cutback of 15 to 20 per cent. There is a slaughter of time and talent. As one medical researcher puts it, "I face the possibility of having to give up my major endeavour of the last eight years. I cannot help but feel personal bitterness at such a prospect". And I, Mr. Speaker, can well understand his bitterness.
It is not just the doctors who are going to be adversely affected by these restrictions, but their technical and support staff as well. It sometimes takes as long as ten years to build up a cohesive team of technicians and doctors and to assemble equipment. If a grant is cut off after a viable working situation exists and then has to be dissipated, how many years are actually wasted? What happens to the personnel and the equipment involved? How can we evaluate the slaughter of hope, the hope that is to be denied many, many people who are afflicted with debilitating diseases for which there are presently no cures? There are no statistics to enumerate the chronically ill or to indicate the degree of suffering which they must endure.
How many Canadians will have to die prematurely from heart disease and cancer, our two major health adversaries, while we withhold medical research funds that could and should be used to push on with research which has been under way in these areas, or to establish new programs to study their cause and cure?
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) tells us that there is no brain drain, that 101 doctors have come from the U.S. to Canada while only 60 have gone the reverse route. Does the minister not take into account those 353 young Canadians who are now working in research fields in the United States and who hold foreign medical visas? That figure was given to me today by the director of special programs in the United States.
The frustration in the ranks of the medical research fraternity is immeasurable. The agony of the "on-again off-again" programming instils such a sense of insecurity that many of our top notch research doctors are simply giving up their hopes of being able to continue their work in Canada and are leaving the country. Submission after submission from medical doctors engaged in conducting research in our universities has indicated that they will not be staying in Canada. We are heading for the second age of the brain drain in Canada. Surely it is a national
Medical Care Act
disgrace that young men and women, graduates of our own schools, are forced to anchor their careers south of the border.
If the government continues to take the shortsighted view that medical research is a frill, a large number of young scientists will have no choice but to stay in the United States, or to leave Canada because of the lack of opportunity to use their highly qualified skills here. Given the current government attitude, Canadian universities cannot continue training and graduating research scientists if there is no future for them in this country. In Canada it is necessary to work out of the universities because there is no central medical research establishment such as exists in many other countries.
We are making involuntary exiles of some of our most promising and responsible citizens of the future. Can we afford this drain on our society? Can we afford to lose the $100,000 it has cost to educate each and every one of these doctors who will not be remaining in or returning to Canada?
What are the priorities of the government? A few days ago representatives of the federal government were sitting down with the provincial premiers. This government announced to them that it wished to cut back on health care. The government has already cut back on health research. I ask you what kind of reasoning this is, because without research to solve some of our medical mysteries how will we ever be able to reduce the cost of health care?
With the spiralling costs of hospital and health care institutions, who can say what a dollar spent today in finding cures will save in ten years? I think a new adage can be coined; we are no longer penny wise and pound foolish, but in this instance we are millions wise and billions foolish. Who can say that billions of future dollars could be saved by present research investment? Who knows what suffering and premature death could be saved by that same investment? When the government speaks about the cost benefit of research, how can it be measured in terms of health and the very lives of people?
In multiple sclerosis alone $200 million is spent each year in caring for victims of this crippling disease and less than $1 million is spent in searching for the cure. Science has proved that it is a virus causative illness, and the President of the MS Association told the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs that the basic research has been done. Now they are ready to move into the more expensive clinical phase but research money is drying up.
How can increases of 25 per cent or more to the Department of National Defence, the Public Service Commission, the Post Office, and the Canadian Radio Television Commission be justified while the Medical Research Council has not even received the 15 per cent increase the government indicated would be allowed for over-all government expenditures? When less than 1 per cent of the total National Health and Welfare budget is allocated to the Medical Research Council, and when its real dollar funding has actually declined by 8 per cent while other federal expenditures have increased by 105 per cent, that is pretty indicative of the status that is placed on explorative medicine.

June 17, 1976
Medical Care Act
The federal government should not have to be convinced of the value of medical research when many of us can remember the time, not so long ago, when tuberculosis, polio, and diabetes were rampant killers. I ask whether the government is truly concerned about the health and wellbeing of Canadian people. If that is the case, then how can we in all conscience say that the emotional and physical health of the present and future population of Canada is only worth $50 million?
The Minister of National Health and Welfare has proposed that we spend $70 million on influenza vaccine during the next year. That is $20 million more than the whole Medical Research Council funds from the federal government. That is $20 million more than the government will put into research for every type of medical problem now being studied, while at the same time one outstanding doctor has had his application for a modest grant to continue his research curtailed. It is conceded that this doctor has achieved a breakthrough in the study of one of the bacteria that can cause meningitis, a disease which has reached epidemic proportions in some countries.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to make a few comments at third reading stage of this particular bill. Let me say at the outset I was extremely interested and really gratified to hear the minister state that the present situation in respect of federal-provincial negotiations is somewhat encouraging. I think he amplified that he is hopeful that those negotiations will come up with a new formula for cost sharing relationships with the provinces. I find this most encouraging, but on the other hand it seems to be somewhat inconsistent with the bill that was introduced.
I want to remind hon. members that, as I understood the purpose of the bill when it was introduced, it was in effect to limit the rate of increase in federal spending on medical care but that there was also the important addition that it was to allow for federal-provincial cost sharing on new alternatives with the development of less expensive health care delivery programs and services. As the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) indicated somewhat earlier, and certainly I concur with this, one must be somewhat suspect concerning the degree of progress which has been made in this particular area. Having said that, I think one also should look the possibility that the minister may well have had an alternative purpose in introducing this particular legislation in view of the encouraging comments he made somewhat earlier, that is, perhaps it was a method to manipulate the provinces in terms of these negotiations.
May I simply say that if the minister is correct in respect of the facts he presented this afternoon, then in fact this entire piece of legislation is redundant. Indeed the particular negotiations which are going on at the present time, if they are as fruitful as the minister indicated, may be far more important than this particular legislation we have before us today.
I wish to make one or two references to the comments made by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. If I may say so, certainly I am in agreement with the theme he developed about the importance of the universal concept of the medicare program. However, I think we must also recognize that there have been some inequities in the program. I think if one were to assess the program now-and the minister has the figures at his disposal-we would find that there is evidence to suggest that the very people we had hoped to reach through this type of program, principally those at the poverty level, have in fact not been reached by this program. So in fact in this universal program there are indeed inequities which exist. I think this is one area to which the minister must direct his attention. I refer to the fact that the great proportion of the medicare program, universal in concept, really has not reached that group of individuals, which was the intent of the program in the initial instance.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands talked about the importance of looking for alternative low-cost programs to replace our high cost programs. Certainly one can sympathize with this. I am sure there are ongoing discussions between the federal and provincial governments. However, I think it is important to bring one matter to the attention of this House, that is, that we must avoid what I call the add-on principle. Certainly if one is
June 17, 1976

replacing a high cost program with a low cost program then indeed one must show that these high cost facilities, this high cost technology, and these highcost projects are indeed replaced by the so-called low-cost type programs.
I think there is a trend from time to time-and I believe, Mr. Speaker, that all of us have seen evidence of this-in which we end up with an add-on principle. In principle it seems nice to have a low-cost program, but if in fact it does not replace the high cost program to which I referred then it has been a failure in terms of economics.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands referred to the minister's new health perspective for Canadians. I want to emphasize that I think this is an important part of the equation of the health care program in Canada. I think this is an area in which the federal government must and should give greater leadership. The hon. member has discussed several aspects in this regard. There are one or two things on which I want to enlarge in a moment in respect of which I think the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) can and should give leadership.
I also agree with the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowi-chan-The Islands when he referred to the problem of attempting to equate health care with economic factors. I would go one step further. I think there is a myth which exists which should be exploded, that is, that good health care can be equated with good health. I think this would be one of the advantages if the minister were prepared to take action along the general tenor of the philosophy that is outlined in the new health perspective.
I wish to make one comment regarding the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) who talked about the introduction of a medicare program in the province of Saskatchewan. I would simply say in passing to him, and I apologize for not remembering the year, that the Canadian Medical Association long before that program was introduced actually proposed a universal program of medicare for Canada which in fact was rejected by the federal government of that day. I am sure if the hon. member is interested I could give him all the details of the facts regarding that particular situation.
As I indicated somewhat earlier, I feel there is an important part of the equation which has been referred to previously in which I believe there should be very strong leadership at the federal level. I would like to refer to some of these areas. Perhaps in the first instance I might come back to what one might refer to as environmental health hazards and environmental health problems which are very numerous. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands referred to some of them.
I believe this House will recall, I think it was on May 7 this year, that there was a debate on mercury poisoning. This really in effect is a prototype of several types of environmental hazards which exist in Canada. Obviously, however, it has had a very devastating effect principally upon the native people in Canada, particularly the Crees in northwestern Quebec and the natives in northwestern Ontario. Let me simply emphasize that over and above the destruction we have seen within these native communities there is no question that the myth that Minamata disease does not exist has been eliminated. I am sure we are all aware that Dr. Barbeau of the Montreal Institute of
Medical Care Act
Neurology, who is well known both nationally and internationally, has demonstrated the presence of Minamata disease among the Cree people, and among two white people in that particular area. As I understand it, there is recent evidence to suggest that there are symptoms among the native people in the northwestern part of Ontario.
The member also mentioned the problem of radiation. Irrespective of my personal concerns about the growth of atomic energy, and particularly in terms of weaponry, I think we also must recognize that there is substantial evidence to point out that radiation itself is a hazard. We have had the recent situation, for example, at Port Hope and Uranium City. I think it must be made very clear that the federal Atomic Energy Board has not clearly established safeguards. We now have well documented evidence that radiation hazards are possible, and certainly do cause illnesses such as cancer, leukemia, and other disease entities. I do not know of one expert who will not say that there is a potential health hazard from the possible radiation effects of uranium. This is another area of course which requires additional research.
The problem of polychlorinated biphenyls, or pcb's, has received a great deal of attention lately, particularly in relation to the smelt in the Great Lakes system. We know that this particular substance is stored in the fatty tissues of individuals, indeed probably stays there for a long period of time, and perhaps indefinitely. We are well aware of the potential health hazards in this particular area.
One other rather interesting aspect is that of birth defects. I think that if one were to look very carefully at the Canadian context the two most common birth defects we see are related to spina bifida anencephalus. Spina bifida is the condition in which the neuro sheath is incompletely formed, and anencephalus implies the incomplete development of the brain. Let me say, without going into details, that it is important to know that there is now a substantial body of evidence to suggest that environmental health factors play a substantial role and are perhaps one of the most important causative factors in this regard.
Somewhat earlier mention was made of asbestos in connection with the pulmonary problems it causes. I should point out that it has not only been a problem in Ontario, but a recent judicial inquiry in the province of Quebec indicated very clearly that approximately 15,000 workers in that province are risking their health each day that they work in the mines. The problems of lead poisoning have been well documented in an excellent report prepared by the province of Ontario in recent months. Carbon monoxide, chlorine, smoke inhalation, various solvents, occupational hazards-all of these are problems which play a most important part in terms of environmental health hazards. There have been new findings with regard to health hazards encountered by polyvinyl workers. A rare form of cancer was recognized at the Goodrich plant in Kentucky. I would remind hon. members that there are now well documented cases of this disease entity in the Canadian context.
I could go on and talk about many other environmental health problems which, in my view, require a great deal of attention, but there are three points that should be made

about environmental health hazards. First, when we talk about environmental health factors this implies that individual Canadians have no control over certain disease entities, and that there must be intervention on the part of the government. I suggest that in the national context leadership should come from the federal government, and a strong role in terms of our health care system implies a far greater involvement by the government in the entire area of environmental health hazards. As I indicated previously, in my view the federal government has the responsibility of demonstrating this leadership.
As indicated earlier, basic research is most important in the area of environmental health because, as has been alluded to, although we have many of the answers in this area, certainly there are many aspects of pollution and environmental implications with which we are not yet familiar.
Having mentioned the area of research perhaps I should make some comment on the direct relationship between the economics of health and the use of basic medical research, despite the fact that a debate was held two days ago on the importance of medical research, and the point was made by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands.
Let me take a moment to compliment the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville on some of the remarks he made earlier, and the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga) on the excellent speech he gave. I am sorry the Minister of National Health and Welfare was not here last Tuesday, but I know he had an excellent excuse for his absence. Perhaps I might make reference to one or two aspects of this subject which I think he would find interesting. I do this, Sir, because I believe that in terms of the total health care system one cannot divorce Bill C-68 from the most important component that was involved, that is, negotiations with a view to finding alternative forms of health care referred to by the minister in the past.
I would like to review briefly the types of technology in medical research because one must understand the importance of research and the part it plays in improving health care. There is an excellent article by Dr. Thomas Lewis from the University of Cornell in which he writes about technology being divided into three broad groups. The first group is the so-called non-technology. This is the type of technology which is most important, what we often refer to as supportive therapy, the sort of care that is used for cases of rheumatoid arthritis, osteo arthritis, cancer, etc. We must recognize that it requires a great deal of money, time, and effort by specialized personnel, whether they be physicians, nurses or paramedical people, and it requires a great deal of money for hospital care. Yet we must recognize that there is no definitive answer in terms of the actual disease mechanism. We do not have an understanding of the disease process.
The second group is referred to as the half-way technology. It is very significant in today's health care. We see it in connection with organ transplants, and the treatment of coronary heart disease in intensive care units. It involves sophisticated types of equipment and highly trained technical personnel. It is obvious that this type of technology is very expensive, and yet I must remind hon. members that it is only half-way technology, something that compen-

sates for the breakdown of a particular organ, something that is used to prolong the life of a patient. But again in these cases we do not have a complete understanding of the disease mechanism. I believe that the public and many members of this House do not fully understand this type of technology.
Every day when we pick up a newspaper we read about some new organ transplant which is interpreted as being a major breakthrough in research. Yet in many respects it is primitive in its approach, and although sophisticated technology is used there is an incomplete understanding of the disease entity.
Third, we have a type of technology which really goes unnoticed, the technology that introduced the antibiotics which in effect eradicated the very severe problem of infectious diseases which occurred in our hospitals many years ago. The other day I gave the example, which is probably worth repeating, of a case of typhoid fever. In terms of the treatment methodology that was used many years ago, a patient with a case of typhoid fever would probably be admitted to hospital for 50 to 60 days, would require intensive, highly skilled nursing care, and a careful monitoring of laboratory tests. The cost of that was astronomical. A conservative estimate would now be about $10,000 to $15,000 in today's terms. What are we talking about today? A case of typhoid fever is treated with a bottle of cloramphemical, with two or three days of fever, after which there is improvement. I would simply emphasize what my colleagues have said previously, that basic medical research has a very direct cost effect relationship over a period of time.
I want to congratulate the minister on the position he has taken with respect to motor vehicle accidents. It is a matter that has concerned me for many years. As the minister well knows, in recent years it has been the leading cause in terms of potential years of life lost in relation to other deaths. The latest figures I have show that back in 1971 there were 5,690 deaths from motor vehicle accidents, a great number of them in the younger age group. As I recall, 50 per cent were in the age group between 15 and 25. I do want to compliment the minister at least for taking some aggressive action regarding motor vehicle accidents, seat belts, speed, etc.
Another matter which might be looked into is that of alcohol and drug abuse. I am sorry that I cannot compliment the minister in this regard. I recognize that he has allowed some funds for-

speechtext:
I am sure I can compliment him for at least a small degree of action with respect to native people, but when one recognizes that there are direct medical costs which exceed the total intake of provincial and federal taxes, which, as I understand, run very close to $1 billion per year, we must recognize that we have a very serious problem on our hands. I want to emphasize that this does not include the indirect costs for loss of work, loss of productivity, family break up, etc. I must remind the minister that, in my opinion, he has not scratched the surface,
June 17, 1976

and a great deal must be done. This is another area which requires federal responsibility and federal leadership.
There is another matter I want to mention in passing. It is related to this whole subject, and I hope it has been discussed at federal-provincial meetings. It is the problem of drug misuse. I am somewhat appalled when I see the amount of drugs used by the average Canadian. From the recent figures I have, Canadians on the average use approximately one million tranquilizers per day. We have to consider the large number of accidental poisonings and overdoses of drugs which take place. The incidence of drug reactions is very high indeed.
There is a good deal of evidence to suggest that somewhere between 5 per cent and 10 per cent of admissions to hospital is really related to the problem of overdoses of drugs and reactions to drugs, and I should remind the minister that in this particular instance there is really a geometrical progression in terms of drugs. In other words, if a person takes two drugs, that does not produce twice the chance for a reaction. It really produces three or four times the probability of a reaction. Of course the more drugs one takes, the greater the propensity for this problem. The minister should be looking at drug misuse very carefully with the provinces, and if there is an area in which leadership at the federal level would fit into the philosophy the minister has described in his new health perspective, obviously this is it.
Another matter concerns me immensely because, in my opinion, the federal government has directed no appreciable attention to it. That is the whole area of mental health. From the limited information which has been obtained from the federal-provincial meetings, I understand that there have been some discussions about this, but I think it is worth while to take a moment to consider the magnitude of this problem. I would like to remind hon. members that approximately four out of every 1,000 Canadians occupy hospital beds because of mental illness at any particular time. I should also point out that there are one million children, or approximatley 5 per cent to 10 per cent of schoolchildren, who suffer from emotional or learning disorders.
I am sure hon. members who have been on school boards or who have been associated with schoolchildren will recognize the effects of dyslexia and learning disorders of all kinds. These youngsters really have the basic innate ability to do just as well as any youngster, and yet we have directed very little or almost no attention to this problem.
We should also recognize that approximately 50 per cent of the time of physicians is devoted to dealing with emotional problems. Here again we have no response from the federal government, and no help in this area. There are innumerable other statistics one could cite in this regard, but let me stress that the federal government has demonstrated no leadership with regard to mental health. That is left entirely to the provincial governments, and I urge the minister to recognize that this is an area which is national in scope. It is a problem which occurs in every province and every territory in Canada, and requires initiative on the part of the federal government and leadership from the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
Our aging people were alluded to earlier, and their problems require leadership at the federal level. We must
Business of the House
recognize that we have a growing population ratio. I recall the present figure, something like 7 per cent of our population is over the age of 65, which represents about 1.7 million people. However, it is also projected that by the mid 1980's somewhere between 9 per cent and 10 per cent of the population will be above this age. If we look very carefully, we will see that a very high percentage of these people utilize hospital beds. The attitude toward these senior citizens is certainly not conducive to an over-all program of rehabilitation or to an over-all program of handling their particular problems. They have more than just medical problems per se, whether they be, for example, arthritic problems or genital urinary problems in females, or muscular problems which are more common in males. However, what we tend to ignore, and have not concentrated sufficient energy on are the psychological problems of senior citizens.
Far too many senior citizens are lonely, far too many are out of the mainstream of society, and far too many live at the poverty level because their incomes have not been adequately supplemented. Far too many live in isolation. A great deal could be done, not only at the community level- and there should be far more community involvement- but also at the provincial level. However, this is the type of problem which is national in scope and demands leadership from the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
Another important area in the delivery of health care is consumer involvement. I have been concerned for some time that in the evolution of our health care system there has been a great deal of misunderstanding with respect to the health care system. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I called it six o'clock I had already developed two or three themes. I have indicated and attempted to describe in some detail the irrelevance of Bill C-68 in terms of the federal-provincial negotiations that are being conducted and have been conducted within the past two or three days. I was attempting to make some reference to the health perspective as introduced by the minister some time ago, particularly in the areas of environmental health, problems relating to the aged, mental health, and several other areas where I think the minister should be showing greater leadership and responsibility than he has demonstrated in the past.
Before terminating my remarks I want to deal again with the health perspective as presented by the minister. As I recall, he developed four categories, one of which was the so-called health organization or management system, environmental health matters, lifestyle health, and the area of biology, recognizing of course that the organizational health area is that traditional area of health that in the past historically, politically, and on a community basis has been a provincial responsibility. There were, of course, the other three areas which I alluded to earlier.
I want to turn now to the so-called organization health aspect which as I indicated is, in my view, and has been a provincial responsibility and to touch on two or three matters with which the minister should have some direct concern and input and should show greater leadership. One area is physician manpower requirements. If one were to assess the situation in Canada there are indications that the physician-patient ratio is adequate, but there is no question that there are inequities in various parts of Canada. For example, if one would look at the rural areas, particularly in the northern parts of Canada, he would find that frequently there are not enough physicians.
It is also important to look at the various types of specialties present in the Canadian context. One frequently finds that there may be an over-abundance of certain specialists. Surgery may fit into this category and yet there may be other areas where there is an urgent need; for example psychiatry, opthalmology, and dermatology are frequently bypassed.
Having said that, I believe there is an immediate need for high level negotiations between the federal and provincial counterparts to achieve certain objectives. It is very important that they should help to define these various health needs, some of which I alluded to a moment ago. It is important that they identify these manpower requirements in terms of geographic location. It would also be useful if they established specialist requirements in all of the areas of post graduate studies. This would be extremely important in giving more diversification across Canada.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Turner).]
It would also be useful to determine the appropriate numbers of specialists needed in the various segments of Canada, certainly in relation to population. They must find means to attempt to encourage physicians to practice in various parts of Canada. Again I refer to those areas such as northern Ontario where in the past there has been an absence of their presence. In this regard it is essential that they look very carefully and re-evaluate the medical schools in Canada to ensure we have the production capability to turn out students which are highly qualified in the Canadian context.
There is another area where the minister could play an extremely important role. I now speak in terms of computer technology. We know there have been rather unfortunate experiences in terms of records. In many instances hospital data is outdated. It is certainly not current in terms of what is happening in Canadian society.
Despite the fact that we had a nutrition survey in the past, we see very little data regarding the health status of Canadians. It is therefore difficult to know the extent of the health problems as they exist on a day to day basis.
It would be useful in this regard if the Minister of National Health and Welfare were to demonstrate some leadership and launch an effective program in this area with adequate help in order to assess the health of Canadians. We would then be far more informed in terms of developing future programs. I have no doubt that, with co-operation from the provinces, we could update and modernize this kind of technology which would give us this kind of information.
Finally I want to refer to what I call the regionalization of health care. We hear a good deal about regional variations regarding health care in Canada. There has certainly been some effort in the past to rationalize the delivery of health care in the various regions of Canada. I think of those so-called depressed or under-privileged areas of Canada. I should emphasize that in the past we on this side of the House have agreed in principle with the concept of community health centres.
In his negotiations with the provinces and in re-defining the new formula in terms of federal-provincial negotiations, the minister must ensure equitable standards across Canada. He must pay very close attention to such provinces as the mari times, and other so-called have- not provinces. In any formula it is absolutely essential that we ensure those provinces have the same standards and universality as the rest of Canada.
I wish to summarize by indicating that Bill C-68 is redundant in terms of the negotiations going on at the present time. Unfortunately it does not address itself to the comprehensive problems we see in the delivery of health care across Canada. I have attempted to allude to many of these problems for which I feel the minister has a direct responsibility and should be providing leadership. I certainly hope that he will take heed of the observations made by many members in this debate today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I very much enjoy participating in this very important debate on health. There is often talk at federal-provincial conferences of readjustment of federal subsidies to the provinces, and in various areas, as was recently the case with respect to health.
In the Montreal La Presse dated June 16, 1976, Mr. Marcel Adam pointed out in very interesting comments summed up in an editorial the results of the attitude of the federal government which continued to drag the provinces into joint programs in the areas of health, social welfare and assistance to post-secondary education whose costs have increased in recent years because of inflationary tensions.
Medical Care Act
The circumstances are appropriate to quote an excerpt from that editorial as follows:
Committed to paying 50 per cent of the cost of those programs the federal government now finds the bill exorbitant, and decided to cut back its financial participation. It feels all the more justified in doing so that it is paying for programs it cannot control from an administrative point of view because they affect areas-health and education-of provincial jurisdiction. There is in that new federalism proposed by Mr. Trudeau something a little annoying because he is amending unilaterally under the law of the strongest the rules of a game that his partners accepted to play on the condition that both parties would respect them. Now that the federal government has exhausted the electoral viability of those joint programs he would like to shift on weaker shoulders a burden in which he does not see anything more than financial embarrassment and political inconvenience.
We all realize that the monetary problem comes into play here and becomes at certain moments a determining factor. It is readily seen that provincial health ministers are interested at the smell of federal dollars. On the other hand, the federal government faced with the problems of inflation and monetary instability is attempting to impose restraints. The results can be disadvantageous from several points of view.
Recently, in a document undoubtedly sent to every member of parliament, the chairman of the medical research group mentioned two specific points that I shall quote:
1.	Research is the sole practical solution to reduce the cost of the various medical services as it enables to develop treatments for diseases affecting thousands of people and costing the government more than $7 billion every year.
2.	The majority of our leading physicians and surgeons are attracted by teaching hospitals with active research programs mostly sponsored by the Medical Research Council. While it allows a general spending increase of about 16 per cent, the government did freeze the budget of the council at the previous year level. This action results in a significant reduction of activities at the medical research level. The greatest scientists have to go elsewhere to continue their research work. This action will have important effects on the quality of medical education throughout the country.
Following the announcement of Bill C-68 concerning the review of federal-provincial agreements in the hospital insurance field and the limitation of credits for the federal contribution to health insurance, the Quebec medical association submitted a brief where it mentioned on the last page, and I quote:
However, if Ottawa persists in its plan to reduce its contribution to health services without giving to the provinces an equivalent transfer of the taxation base we think that the provinces would be encouraged to impose a deterrent fee to medicare consumers or to use private insurance companies to insure the difference in the medicare costs that the federal does not seem in a position to support any more.
Health is a basic right for every citizen. In principle, this right has been recognized for many years; in practice, however, it was violated since medical treatments were available only to some people within society. Since then, the state has intervened. I am not in favour of public-controlled medical services. However, considering that a large percentage of the people were and still are assisted in one way or another by welfare agencies and that many workers have suffered from endless unemployment periods, considering further the inadequate wages of a number of heads of families, the state felt it necessary to direct this legislation in such a way as to enable everybody to enjoy a good health which present medical knowledge allow us to have.

June 17, 1976
Medical Care Act
These are in short the reasons which contributed to the implementation of medicare plans. However, it has to be noted that no concensus was reached to determine what would be the best service: federal or provincial, comprehensive or partial, universal or restricted, compulsory or voluntary. And how many other things should be specified, how many other questions would have to get an answer, among which the following which is of vital importance: Who will pay? To whom? And how?
On several occasions, during the debates which led to the implementation of the present socializing medicare plans, we had submitted proposals which were probably not complicated enough to deserve the attention of the politicians of the time, or too realistic according to their usual idea of administrative difficulties which arise from the different plans in effect. We had suggested that the state might contribute through an assistance at the level of insurance premiums which would have enabled every citizen or group of citizens to select the medicare policy which would suit them best. Based on the Social Credit Party's proposals, the medicare plan would have been more easily implemented, more comprehensive and less costly, while securing everybody's safety with no obligations to all parties concerned. Unhappily, the government opted for a medicare plan prepared by bureaucrats who have complicated things.
Following a lengthy period of hesitation when it was sometimes difficult to determine whether we had a sickness medical care insurance or the sickness of insurance, we finally contracted the sickness of socializing insurance. We all agree on the common objective: access for everyone to every form of medical care. However we realized that a number of difficulties had risen when time came to determine the conditions to be applied.
I want to point out in passing that the health care plans have contributed precious little towards training more physicians, even though people are complaining of a lack of physicians. To remedy this situation, two solutions presented themselves; either train more physicians or allow other persons to take part in dispensing some medical treatments and relieve the physicians from a number of chores. The medical profession has not taken up any of these solutions with regard to the possible cooperation of other professions. We all know the attitude physicians are taking faced with chiropractors, optometrists and even pharmacists.
Health is priceless. So is the service that restores it. Yet most doctors manage to use that imponderable to their advantage. In the newspaper La Presse dated April 18, 1966, a journalist quotes the testimony given by Dr. Benoit Deshaies at a seminar on proverty, and I quote:
Protected by some politicians and constituted into a real bourgeois and priviledged cast, oblivious to social ills, a minority of some 15 per cent of all doctors, whose income fluctuates between $75,000 and $100,000, rule as masters, at the expense of the population, on an empire: that of their profession and the medical organization.
Too often, qualified and willing students cannot have access to the courses that would allow them to complete their training as medical doctors. The number of candidates seems to be controlled by an organization that wishes to keep its monopoly in the field. If we add to that the

disastrous effects of extended strikes which finally penalize defenceless patients, we get a rather dark picture of the result of the various health insurance plans. Those urging undiscriminate change must recognize that too quick a conversion of methods has serious disadvantages.
I have here today's issue of La Presse, from which I quote a paragraph concerning hospital admission problems:
The President of the Council of Physicians, Dr. Paul Henri Royer, noted there were two very serious cases of heart trouble but only one can be cared for. So the younger was treated. We were thus faced with irrational choices.
This is what is happening. I also read in La Presse of July 30, 1975 an article titled:
Yesterday's and today's medicine.
That article was signed by Dr. Leo Ladouceur, who has this to write concerning today's medicine, and I quote:
Today's medicine is capable of extraordinary things that used to be unthinkable. It is in its every day practice that it has become inefficient, and even harmful.
Who is responsible for that state of affairs? The article gives the following answer:
The government, the patient and the physician. The government, by establishing free care for everybody. What was needed was free care for have-nots, leaving the majority of the people with the obligation to pay a small part of the cost of medical care. This would have prevented abuses, avoiding that physicians' offices be literally invaded by patients with either imaginary or benign sores. Under current conditions physicians do not have the time or enough of it to get interested in those who are really ill. There is no way to prevent clients from going from one physician to another to ensure that the first diagnosis was the right one, and the first prescription the right one, to prevent that imaginary patients besiege waiting rooms and examination rooms because the program is free. The physician, obsessed by the idea of making money and who hands out medicine like a dry good merchant. One patient every ten minutes, assembly line medicine, where symptoms are treated instead of illness. Diagnosis means an investigation, therefore questions and answers, an examination, X-rays, laboratory analyses and monitoring to correct your mistakes or confirm your forecasts. And the poor physician, not as consciencious or tired out, with clouded cerebral processes, makes out a prescription for drugs which are effective, but sometimes contradictory. This is what can come from good intentions and an, extraordinary level of science, which is nevertheless necessary.
In another paragraph entitled "Castonguette or Char-gex", he adds the following:
As much respect as I have for today's surgery and medicine, with its examination, diagnosis, excision and transplant methods, which bring back yesterday's surgeons to the exhalted barbers that they once were, today's medicine is too often practised in doctors' offices where patients pass through at rates that the Medicare Control Board would like to see increased and come out with hastily written but duly signed prescriptions for a series of drugs which are highly effective, sometimes contradictory and capable of bringing a dead man back to life or killing someone.
In view of the present results, of the application terms, of medicare plans, of the many formalities resulting from this bureaucratic system, of the total or partial paralysis of services due to multiple strikes in this area like elsewhere, it is rather difficult to foresee where this expensive and unstable system will lead us.
In closing, to illustrate certain events that can happen, I would like to quote a passage from an editorial of the CJRC station dated March 15, 1971, and entitled:

speechtext:
A good family man, when seeing that his sick daughter was not getting any better, desperately tried to have a doctor come to his home. Exasperated by the many refusals of the doctor who told him dryly to take his daughter, to wrap her in a blanket and to bring her to him, the father did as he was told even though the temperature was freezing cold.
A few days later, in the middle of the night and during a cold spell, the doctor's furnace broke down. He looked in the yellow pages to find a heating specialist. He finally reached one who, it happened, was the father of the sick girl of a while ago. Recognizing the voice of the doctor, the plumber-father paid his nighttime customer in his own coin, saying: Take your furnace, wrap it up in a blanket and bring it in to me.
Doubtless, the doctor concerned learned a good lesson. Several ailing persons have had to wait interminably before being hospitalized, and the application of health insurance plans complicated the situation. It would be a good idea to come back to good old common sense. That may be one of the virtues we lack most in our era of insecurity in various fields.

Mr. Speaker, I hope I can meet expectations. speechtext: The Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Blais) says it was the courts that did it. I would disagree completely with him. The courts may have made some input, but I am sure it was the persuasion of members like the hon. member for Spadina and the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Martin) who have spoken out about the closing of hospitals across Ontario that had a direct effect on the Ontario minister of health.
