maintopic: A TELLING STORY ABOUT HUMAN NATURE
speechtext:
None of us wants any person to have a heart attack, but I am sure that the minister of health for Ontario as a result of that heart attack had second thoughts with regard to closing of hospitals. I would not wish that the present Minister of National Health and Welfare should have a heart attack, but I hope he will have a change of heart with regard to Bill C-68. It is very important that he have that change.
This has been quite a week, Mr. Speaker. On Monday we had the premiers of the provinces meeting with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) trying to work out problems with respect to equalization payments for health and education.
I am sure you will remember that on Tuesday we had a Progressive Conservative motion condemning the government for its funding of medical research. I asked at that time whether there was a doctor in the House. There were many doctors in the House, some of whom spoke on that subject. Many laymen also spoke, and most were very critical about the cutbacks in medical research grants across the country. They realize how important medical research grants are if we are to maintain a high standard of health across Canada. We now have, and it seems to be very timely, the third reading stage of Bill C-68 which deals with health and contributions by the federal government toward health costs incurred by the provinces.
We heard many speeches during second reading of this bill and we had many amendments at the report stage. Before this bill passes I am sure we will hear many speeches on third reading. As a result I hope the minister will have a change of heart and a change of attitude. In my February speech I said I always considered him a man of compassion, and a man of high intelligence who could carry some of his ideas in respect of social needs into legislation. However, I have been bitterly disappointed by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and bitterly disappointed by his parliamentary secretary who has been unable to persuade the minister.
It is my hope that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Marchand), who gave me such healthy applause at the beginning, is able to persuade his colleague in cabinet regarding the contents of Bill C-68. That minister was at the Habitat conference, and I shared some of my time there with him. He is a person who is concerned about human settlements. When we talked about human settlements we were talking about housing, about water, about health and the environment. We spoke about all these subjects at the conference. It was my hope that the Minister of the Environment, after meeting many of the delegates there, would have had a change in attitude and heart, and come back and impose the moral tone in the cabinet that Sister Theresa imposed at the conference in Vancouver.
One thing I like about the Minister of the Environment is that he is a man of very high moral fibre. The minister has been a representative of labour throughout his life. He made the decision to join the Liberal party, which I think was wrong, but he made it. He has had a certain input in some legislation, although it has not been much. I hope he will be able to change the attitude of the Minister of National Health and Welfare regarding this particular bill so that he can put legislation on the books of Canada that will be acceptable. I hope the Minister of the Environment will put legislation on the books in respect of the environ-

June 17, 1976
Medical Care Act
ment and pure water. It is only men like the Minister of the Environment who can persuade other ministers. I have noticed some nodding applause from some of the ministers regarding my statement about the minister's strength, calibre, and intelligence. The Minister of National Health and Welfare is not here tonight, so I hope the Minister of the Environment will take the message to him that I hope to convey in the next 20 to 25 minutes regarding Bill C-68.
It is my belief that the Minister of the Environment is not fully aware of the contents of this bill. It is a complex piece of legislation and I wish to read some of its contents very slowly. Under the Medical Care Act the federal government contributes to provincial medical care insurance plans on the basis of 50 per cent of the per capita cost for the year of all new insured services provided under the provincial plan, multiplied by the average for the year of the number of insured persons in the province at the end of each month. That just indicates how complex the calculation is in respect of health care expenses experienced across the country.
This bill would also limit the increase in the federal contribution to the provinces. It imposes a maximum yearly percentage increase in contributions for 1976-77 of 14.5 per cent, for 1977-78 of 12 per cent, and for 1978-79 and thereafter of 10 per cent. These maximum increases include an amount of 1.5 per cent for the increase in the population of the provinces, and if a province grows in population by more than 1.5 per cent the minister has said the maximum increase would be adjusted upwards accordingly. He said that in a speech he made on September 15, 1975, in Montreal. That indicates how complex this medical care bill is, and it also indicates how slowly we must move in respect of making changes.
One of the best contributions I could make on third reading would be to impress upon the Minister of the Environment and the parliamentary secretary what has been set forth by the Canadian Association of University Teachers at the conference held on Monday and Tuesday. When the first ministers discussed health and education the Canadian Association of University Teachers issued a statement in which it was suggested that, before any changes are made regarding equalization payments for post-secondary education, there should be a royal commission established to study the problems of education across the country. This association said this was necessary to establish national standards of education and to maintain the high quality of education in this country.
I was rather proud that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) moved a motion under Standing Order 43 asking the House for unanimous consent regarding a recommendation of the Canadian Association of University Teachers that a royal commission be set up to study education before any changes are made to equalization payments. Perhaps we could apply that type of recommendation to health costs so that before any change is made in equalization payments there would be a royal commission set up to study health costs across this country. Surely that is a reasonable request by a reasonable person to reasonable people. I am sure the ministers would accept that proposition.
Why do I say that? You will remember that back in 1958 when the hospitalization bill was passed this gave all the

provinces the right to contribute or to participate in contributions regarding national health care costs. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that there was a loophole in that bill. Who closed that loophole? It was closed by the Conservative party. Not only that, but the Conservative party under the leadership of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) set up a royal commission on health under Mr. Justice Emmett Hall.
It was the Royal Commission on Health under Mr. Justice Hall which laid the foundation for the legislation on medicare which was set forth in 1968 by Mr. Pearson. We owe a great debt to Mr. Justice Hall in respect of the report of the health committee of 1960-61. At the present time we are now acting on another report of Mr. Justice Hall in respect of the railway unions. It looks as if we will have peace with regard to the railway unions across Canada as a result of the recommendations of Mr. Justice Hall. We have in Mr. Justice Hall a man who has studied the question of health in depth. Surely it behooves us to request Mr. Justice Hall to set up another commission to study health.
Why is there the need for a royal commission on health to be chaired by Mr. Justice Hall? The reason is plain. Only hospital and medical expenses are covered under the present Medical Care Act. This does not include paramedical expenses, pharmacare expenses, dentacare expenses, and the expense of medical appliances. At this stage it is the provinces which bear the cost in respect of paramedical services, pharmacare, dental care, and medical appliances. Surely the cost of $1.5 billion to all the provinces across the nation is an indication of the necessity that these things be included in a national hospital and medicare program. We need national standards. National standards have been established in respect of medical and hospital care. We need an expansion of this type of standard to include paramedical care, pharmacare, dental care, and medical appliances.
Let me turn for a moment to the question of paramedical care. Perhaps I might mention the Habitat Conference. At that conference many films were shown. There was a film shown by the Republic of China. It was called "The Barefoot Doctors in China". For 15 minutes the film set forth the excellent work the barefoot doctors in China are doing in meeting some of the needs that can be met by paramedics across the country. The average doctor will tell you that a great deal of his time is spent doing things that nurses and paramedic people could do just as well and just as efficiently.
That film, "The Barefoot Doctors in China", indicated the type of work that is being done. These people conduct preliminary examinations; they prepare certain drugs from herbs and give out medicines to the people. They also keep records. Some of them give acupuncture treatments. This allows the regular doctors to perform some of the more necessary functions. In China these paramedics are trained in one and one-half to two years. Surely in Canada we should have paramedics playing an important role in the field of national health care.
We talk about national standards. National standards are required in relation to pharmacare. It is only some of the
June 17, 1976

NDP governments across the country which have provided pharmacare as part of their medicare program.
Perhaps I might relate a personal experience in respect of dental care. I have three children. They all required immediate orthodontal care. I had to pay $900 for each child. I am able to afford the $900 for each of my children. I was happy that their teeth were straightened out. This gave them confidence and a better appearance. However, there are many people across this country who cannot obtain orthodontal care. Therefore it is necessary to establish dental care and pharmacare as part of our national standard in respect of our health and medicare programs.
I notice that the Minister of National Health and Welfare is now in his seat. I hope he will listen to this, because when we talk about national standards and compare provinces like Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and British Columbia with some of the have-not provinces such as the maritimes and Newfoundland it becomes apparent how necessary it is that national standards be provided and that these services be available to people who do not have the money to buy them.
First it is necessary to determine what should be included in health care. Second, the question arises concerning who should bear the burden because at the moment in respect of health and medical care there is a sharing between the federal and provincial governments. I ask the minister to give some thought to this. I also ask the hon. member for Spadina to give some thought to this because I am sure he will be speaking on this subject. It may be that we need a national program with regard to medical and health care across the country in the same way we have a national pension plan and a national unemployment insurance plan.

Surely I have aroused the minister and persuaded him and his cabinet colleagues, the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of the Environment, to take a second look at our medicare legislation to determine what they are going to do. I suggest that the time we have had this bill around indicates that it is a bad bill. Indeed there have been times when the government itself considered not proceeding with it, and whenever we have had a chance to debate it in the House, in committee, and now back in the House, we have done our best to persuade the government that the bill should not be proceeded with at all.
Lest my reference to Mr. Turner's announcement of June 23, 1975, suggests that we have been debating the bill all that time, I might put one or two other dates on the record. Bill C-68 was actually introduced and given first reading shortly after that. The date was July 8, 1975. However, the government in its shame about the bill did not seek to move second reading of it until January 28, 1976, so the actual debating of this bill in parliament spans just the last five months.
We have said on every occasion on which it has been possible to do so that in our view this is a bad piece of legislation. There were times when we thought that the government would decide that its anti-inflation program, for what it was worth, was good enough and that this bill did not need to be proceeded with, and there were other times when we thought we were persuading the government that the bill should be withdrawn, but here we are at third reading with the government still trying. However, as is obvious to the government, we are still trying to get across the message that this is legislation which ought not to be passed by the parliament of Canada.
I referred to Mr. Turner's announcement in his budget speech of June 23, 1975.

speechtext:
But Mr. Turner introduced that budget on June 23. He announced not only the proposal to bring in this bill to amend the Medical Care Act, but he also gave the provinces of Canada a five year notice of the termination of the agreements under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act.
It has taken us an exceedingly long time in this country to get legislation in the health and medical field, but I believe a good deal can be said about it in its favour. I think we have made tremendous progress, but what really disturbs me-and any hon. members who paid any attention to the speech I made on second reading will know what is in my mind-is that it was in 1919 that the great Liberals of that day first promised that something would be done about health insurance. It took us about half a century to get it out of the Liberals and, as I have already intimated, the kind of legislation we got from the Liberals, with a great deal of input from other parties, other persons and outside agencies, was not bad. The reason it was not bad was because of certain principles that were locked into the legislation, namely, universality and the attempt to
Medical Care Act
structure it in such a way that Canadians would get the benefit of our health legislation on equal terms no matter where they might live in Canada.
One of the problems that we in this country must yet solve if we are going to have national unity, if we are going to have one Canada, is that of achieving economic levels and service levels that are the same right across the country. All Canadians should enjoy the same standard of living no matter what province they live in. That is one of the real problems of Canadian identity and Canadian unity.
The Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act and the Medical Care Act both paid their respects to this goal by providing that the federal contribution to hospital costs and medical costs would be of the order of 50 per cent of those costs in the provinces, the goal being not just to help provincial governments with their problems but the goal being to establish the same level of hospital and medical services for Canadians wherever they might live. I think it is this kind of thing, the same level of hospital and health services anywhere in Canada, the same level of old age pension benefits-when I began this speech my friend across the way said he hoped I would get pensions into it, so there it is.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
maintopic: A TELLING STORY ABOUT HUMAN NATURE
speechtext: It is the same speech as in 1959.

maintopic: A TELLING STORY ABOUT HUMAN NATURE
speechtext: My hon. friend says it is the same speech as in 1959. Where was he for the 17 years before that? I have been making this kind of speech in the House since 1942 and, if necessary, I shall keep on making it until 1999. I say the things that have done the most for Canadian unity and establishing in Canadians a pride in being part of this country are in this social legislation field-health insurance, family allowances, unemployment insurance, hospital and medical services.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: A TELLING STORY ABOUT HUMAN NATURE
speechtext: And CNR pensions.

maintopic: A TELLING STORY ABOUT HUMAN NATURE
speechtext:
My hon. friend wants to get pensions into it too-CNR pensions and the CPR pensions are areas where we have not yet got things to be as proud of as we should like. My point is, however, that we have progressed. We have moved in a civilized direction by getting these services on the same level for our people in this country wherever they might live. One of the tools used to achieve that has been for the federal government to put what was admittedly a generous input into these services as represented by the so-called or roughly 50 per cent formula.
Tonight we are not dealing with the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, the Old Age Security Act or the Family Allowances Act; we are dealing with the Medical Care Act. The Medical Care Act, as passed by the parliament of Canada after half a century of our struggling for it, provided and still provides that the federal treasury will pay 50 per cent of certain defined costs for certain insured health services in the provinces. That was good- good not in the sense that it helped provincial governments with their financial problems, but good in the kind of health security it provided for Canadians in all parts of

June 17, 1976
Medical Care Act
this land. What does this bill do, Mr. Speaker? It changes that formula; it jeopardizes that important principle that provided for federal financial participation to the tune of 50 per cent. It does it by a new formula which is precise for a couple of years, and then is as uncertain as it can possibly be.
When we debated this bill in the House at second reading, or in committee where we had it for a long time, the spokesmen for the government side tried to counter our arguments by saying that there would be more federal dollars put into health services this year than were put in last year and there could well be still more dollars the year after that. They asked why we say there is any cutback. What one has to do, Mr. Speaker, is not compare this year with last year, or next year with this year, but to compare what will be the story next year under the new legislation with what it would have been under the old legislation.
The old legislation said the federal treasury would pay 50 per cent of the health care costs of the provinces. The new legislation, under this bill if it passes, will say that the federal government will pay the lesser of two quantities; either it will pay the 50 per cent of the provinces' cost or it will pay last year's cost escalated by a certain fixed percentage. If the costs go up more than that percentage the result is that the provinces will get less than 50 per cent of what their health costs are in the current fiscal year or the one that follows this.
There is no question about it, Mr. Speaker. Even though there may be extra dollars in one year compared with a former year, the fact of the matter is that the provinces are being told that they are almost certainly not going to get the 50 per cent which has been the rule-the 50 per cent which enticed them to come into it, the 50 per cent which provided some reasonable guarantee that Canadians would get the same level of health care in any part of Canada. We regard this as a most regressive step. That is why we have done everything we could to persuade the government not to proceed with the legislation. That is why we have played our part in keeping it around for a full year, and if we have our way it will not be passed into law at all.
I said that the bill provides for precise limits that the federal government will pay to the provinces in this fiscal year 1976-77 and for the next one, 1977-78. After that there is no formula in the bill. When it was first brought in there was a percentage there and the government said, "We will be very nice and take that interest percentage out." Instead there was put in a right for the government to fix the percentages of increases that will be allowed after these two years by order in council. Sir, that means that the government will make the decision itself. That means it is a cabinet decision. The provinces can make their representations, there can be consultations-we had that in the Conference Centre on Monday and Tuesday of this week and everyone knows what the provinces felt about those consultations-but they have no input. Parliament has no input.
The government will be free in the fiscal years after the end of March, 1978, to determine unilaterally how much it will cut down on health care revenues for the provinces. The result of this is going to be that the provinces will be getting less than the 50 per cent which brought them into the scheme-the 50 per cent which, while not a sacred

figure in itself, has meant a useful contribution to the implementation of the principle that health care should be the same for Canadians all over Canada whatever province they may live in.
In the process of putting in this provision for future years to be governed by order in council, the government acted as though it wanted to be kind to the Tory party which felt that this should somehow come back to parliament. Therefore into the bill was written the provision which states that after the government has passed an order in council fixing a limit on federal contributions to the provinces in the years in the future, if 50 members of the House of Commons sign a motion calling for the matter to be debated, it shall be debated in the House of Commons right away.
If a motion is put down by those 50 members wanting an order in council to be revoked, if that motion is passed in this House and also in the Senate, then that order in council gets revoked. However, what chance does such a motion have of getting passed in the House of Commons or the Senate dominated by a government with a majority, a government which uses that majority in the way it is used by the government that is across the way?
The provisions in this bill about reference of these future percentage limits to parliament are really a farce. The whole business is thrown into a state of great uncertainty. In particular it is a matter of uncertainty for the provinces. They do not know what the score is going to be in the future. They do not know what the limits will be on federal contributions. They do not know how to plan their health services for the years ahead simply because of the uncertainty that is in this bill.
If this creates uncertainty for the provincial governments, that means in the end it creates uncertainty for the citizens of our various provinces. They may not feel it as quickly as the provincial governments, but they will feel it where it hurts. Somewhere down the line the poorer provinces, once they find the government not providing 50 per cent of the money, will have to resort either to extra charges such as special taxes, deterrent fees or what have you, or to cutting down on health care services. That is a real possibility. Flowing from this bill is a picture of Canada retreating from the high ideal of one nation from coast to coast in which the health care services for our people are to be the same right across the land.
My friend across the way says this is the same speech I have been making since 1959. I realize the hon. member is a young man. He does not realize what was going on before then, although he was in the department and he should have known. Some of us were preaching this kind of thing long before that. Apparently we will have to keep at it for a long while yet.
The point I am trying to make, and I may have said this in 1959 or 1942, or I may have to say it in 1999, is that it is not just a matter of dollars and cents. It is not just a case of one group of cabinet ministers in Ottawa not being concerned about the financial problems of groups of cabinet ministers in Toronto, Winnipeg, Victoria and so on. What is at stake here is the whole concept of Canadian unity, which I submit calls for far more than our hearing
June 17, 1976

the same radio and television programs, enjoying the same football or hockey games, solving our language problems, or what have you.
The surest way to provide some unity and establish pride in being a Canadian anywhere in this country is to ensure that the basic needs of our people are met on the level of equality. If we cannot do it right away in everything, we can do it in terms of health and medical care. I deplore as strongly as I can a measure that is certain to have the effect of creating differences in the levels of health and medical care in the various parts of this country.
Criticisms have sometimes been levelled about speakers not staying close to the bill. I have tried to talk about the bill before us, Bill C-68, which amends the Medical Care Act. However, I think I am entitled to refer to it in the context of things that are related to it.
As I pointed out earlier, when Mr. Turner brought down his last budget on June 23, 1975, he made, amongst other announcements, two in that same budget that related to health. One was that the Medical Care Act would be amended as the government is now trying to amend it. The other was that the provinces were then being told that in five years the agreements under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act would be terminated.
These two things have to be taken together. If it was only medical care that was being changed, maybe the provinces could adjust to it. However, when the provinces are told that not only will they have to handle their health and medical care costs with less help from the federal treasury but they will have to provide their hospital services at this point not knowing what they are going to get from the federal government when the five year period is over, you throw the whole business into a state of jeopardy. When you add to that the kind of thing that was put before the provinces and the country by the federal government at the Conference Centre on Monday and Tuesday of this week, you create a situation that is serious for the future of this land.
I have not had time to read everything that was said, even those things of which copies have been given to us, at the Conference Centre on Monday and Tuesday. However, I read enough of what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said to note that he thinks the federal government, the Liberal party, have done enough because they have played a part in getting hospitalization, medical care, and improved post-secondary education established in this country.
The Prime Minister is almost proud of the fact that his government, and governments before his, gave the money to get these things going. He seems to think that is all the federal government needs to do. I say to the Prime Minister that this is not a static matter. It is not something that comes to an end. You do not just bring proper hospitalization and medical plans into effect and reasonable assistance in the field of education, drop all this, and expect that they will carry on. They will only carry on if there is a formula which provides money from the place where money is most available, and which provides money of the kind that will achieve as much equality as possible right across the country.

The Prime Minister also said at the conference that the desire for the same level of service should not simply become a case of our having a stereotype situation right across the country. In my opinion that was just a rationalization, an excuse for backing off.
Any Liberal in this House who is a Liberal, any Liberal who has respect for what his forbears forecast in 1919, any Liberal who has respect for the dreams and hopes which Mr. Mackenzie King had and which Mr. St. Laurent had, and which Mr. Pearson tried to carry forward, should be mortally ashamed of the steps proposed in this bill as well as in the accompanying termination of the hospital agreements and in the fiscal plan proposed on Monday and Tuesday at the premiers' conference, because these things they are doing amount to turning their backs on the sense of national unity which former Liberals possessed.
I remember-it was a personal conversation but that is no reason why I cannot recall it-being at the United Nations in London in 1945-46. The leader of the Canadian delegation to the preparatory commission was Mr. Dana Wilgress, and then when the first session got going in 1946 the leader was Louis St. Laurent, who was then either minister of justice or the secretary of state for external affairs, later prime minister.

maintopic: A TELLING STORY ABOUT HUMAN NATURE
speechtext: How long was he prime minister?

maintopic: A TELLING STORY ABOUT HUMAN NATURE
speechtext:
Long enough to do a lot more good than is happening now. The time came when some of us were hoping the deliberations would come to an end. Mr. St. Laurent said he hoped the UN session would end soon because he wanted to get back to Canada. The 1945 federal-provincial conference had been something less than a success. I remember him saying, "We can't go on when the advantages for our people are so uneven in different parts of the country." This was the kind of dream some of those Liberals had. Mr. St. Laurent had it; Mr. Pearson had it. They wanted to round out their promises concerning old age security, labour legislation, and adequate provisions in the areas of health and welfare. This meant involving the federal government and the federal treasury so that we might have unity from coast to coast.
The present Prime Minister and his cabinet colleagues are now saying, "We were just getting things going; we got the provinces into these things to do the job and now we propose to back away and let them carry the load." Mr. Speaker, the wealthier provinces can carry it and perhaps provide even better levels of service than their people have enjoyed up to this time. But Canadians in the less wealthy provinces will suffer set-backs and cuts. This will not be good for Canada. That is why we are so strongly opposed to this bill.
As I may have said earlier, if this bill were the only one of its kind maybe the provinces could absorb the shock. Even then we would say that the legislation was wrong. We have said so right from the night Mr. Turner announced it on June 23, 1975. It is still our hope that the bill will be dropped as far as this session of parliament is concerned, at least. But when you consider the fact that the hospital agreements are to be terminated five years

June 17, 1976
Medical Care Act
from last June, and when you add to that the new fiscal arrangements the government is trying to foist on the provinces, and when you add to that the fact that the government is cutting back funds for medical research, the point comes at which one is tempted to ask the question: what is a federal government for? Surely its purpose in a country such as ours is to bring the standards of our people up to the same level from coast to coast, particularly in services which really matter.
I submit that nothing matters more than health and education, and these are the things the federal government has been attempting to cut back this week by the proposals made to the conference on Monday and Tuesday, and health services in particular are damaged by the bill which is now before us. I therefore reiterate our party's determined opposition to Bill C-68. In our opinion it should not pass.

speakeroldname: Miss Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
maintopic: A TELLING STORY ABOUT HUMAN NATURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us today another element of the government's so-called restraint program. I say "so-called" because this, like so many other aspects of that program, is not restraint at all but rather, intergovernmental buck-passing.
What the federal government is proposing to do is limit the growth in its per capita contributions to the provinces under the Medical Care Act to 13 per cent in this fiscal year, to 10.5 per cent in 1977-78, and to a percentage to be determined by the cabinet in subsequent years. The minister assures us that the cabinet-and for once I trust the government's assurances in the field of federal provincial relations will be worth the paper they are printed on-will set the percentage caps for the years after 1977-78 in accordance with an appropriate formula to be developed after consultation with the provincial governments. But that assurance itself is a hollow one because there is no commitment to negotiate this formula with the provinces, merely a pledge to talk with them about it before it is introduced.
The question before us, Mr. Speaker, is whether this unilateral arbitrary action by the federal government is going to hold down the cost of health services to the taxpayer. Most certainly it will hold down the share which appears in the federal estimates, but if we are merely transferring the burden to the provincial level there is no saving to the taxpayer.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) has argued that this bill will provide the provinces with an incentive to hold down the cost of the program because the federal government will no longer be around to pick up half the cost of any increases over the guidelines. That is a clever argument, but it ignores two important facts. First, the provinces already have a strong incentive to hold down costs. After all, they pay a varying but substantial share of the cost of these programs, just as the federal government does. Moreover, it removes the incentive to poorer provinces to close the gap between their per capita expenditures for medical care and those of the more affluent provinces.
Let me quote from the statement of the minister of health for Prince Edward Island, Catherine Collbeck, at

the Victoria conference of provincial ministers of health in August, 1975:
The implementation of Bill C-68 would have a very serious effect on the level of health care in Prince Edward Island ... Our resources are severely strained to meet the rising costs with federal contributions under the present agreement.
Under the new proposal-
That is, Bill C-68.
-it will be difficult to maintain the present standards of health care services with no hope of ever attaining the national standard.
That, Mr. Speaker, from a Liberal health minister in the province of Prince Edward Island! Any real financial restraint that we will obtain under this bill-that is, financial restraint imposed on the provinces as a result of these caps or ceilings-will be purchased at the cost of locking in existing regional disparity in health care. The federal government will bear responsibility for that, but it designed the bill so that the provinces will have to accept the lion's share of the blame. It is the federal government's responsibility, Mr. Speaker, but it shifts the blame to the provincial level, and that is the meaning that the government attaches to the phrase "co-operative federalism."
I note that the minister has made a modest amendment to Mr. Turner's original proposal in that provinces, with the consent of the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the sanction of the federal cabinet may extend insured services without the increased costs which are attributable to those services being subject to the guidelines. A wise and generous use of that power by the minister and his colleagues might provide a measure of benefit to have-not provinces, but because medical services in Canada are already comprehensive the benefit will be slight at best.
On Tuesday in this House the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) argued that his proposed new financing arrangements for the established programs of hospital insurance, medical care, and post-secondary education would benefit the have-not provinces because the principle of equal per capita grants means a larger contribution from the federal treasury to their coffers. That was the Prime Minister's statement in this House.
I hope he is right and I wish he had allowed the premiers of the have-not provinces to test his hypothesis this week by revealing to them the financial details of his proposal. Instead it remains locked in secrecy. He is once again playing his old shell game of what comes next. However, in the field of medical care that program, whatever its merits, is still at least two years in the future. In the meantime this bill could do serious damage to the principle of national standards in health care services and will certainly leave a legacy of bitterness and frustration with the provincial governments. I would say to the minister that that kind of legacy does not augur well for the future of Confederation.

subtopic: INDUSTRY-TEXTILES-REQUEST FOR TABLING OF REPORT OF CLOTHING AND TEXTILE BOARD ON POLYESTER YARN

speakeroldname: Mr. A. D. Alkenbrack (Frontenac-Lennox and Addington):
subtopic: INDUSTRY-TEXTILES-REQUEST FOR TABLING OF REPORT OF CLOTHING AND TEXTILE BOARD ON POLYESTER YARN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight at the adjournment session to bring again to the attention of the government and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson) the precarious position of the Canadian textile industry and of the depressed markets for Canadian textiles at the present time. This depressed and adverse condition particularly applies to the makers of polyester yarn and filament. My words tonight are, of course, pursuant to my question asked of the minister on June 11. I asked it because of my deep concern for the welfare of the industry in my riding.
Celanese Canada, with its plant at Millhaven, is a major employer in my constituency and the area around it, as well as in Kingston, but because of the exposure of its product to the competition from cheap labour from Asiatic competitors overseas, the company has been forced to make major lay-offs in its personnel. This has naturally resulted not only in protests to the government by this great Canadian producer but also has brought sharp protests to the government from the county council of Lennox and Addington. I also have letters from employees and from the reeve and council of the Township of Ernestown.
Let me quote this resolution moved by councillor Grant Mcllquham seconded by councillor Ian Wilson:
Be it resolved that the Council of the Corporation of the Township of Ernestown express concern to the federal Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce regarding the depressed state of the Canadian textile industry resulting from excessive volumes of imported textile products. The impact of this recently resulted in the lay-off of 235 employees from our local Celanese of Canada plant situated in the Township of Ernestown. In addition delay in expansion programs involving upwards of 40 million dollars has resulted. To date 360 employees of synthetic fibre producing plants have been laid off in the Kingston area. Potential summer employment opportunities in the area for upwards of 385 students have also failed to materialize.
Needless to say, this motion was carried by the township council unanimously, and it is strengthened by a personal letter I received from Mr. Mcllquham in the same vein.
There is no doubt about the seriousness of the situation. There are some strange anomalies abroad in the Trudeau government. Why is the minister hesitating? The answer I got to my question on last Friday was that a report would be tabled on the matter of the dumping of cheap textiles into our market from other countries, and that this report would be tabled at the end of June. The end of June means that this House will be adjourned and the government, the cabinet, and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce can then go back to sleep. The House will not be sitting, the government will be rid of the opposition, and generally eased of any further pressure from this belea-

June 17, 1976
Adjournment Debate
guered Canadian industry. That is not a good enough answer for me, Mr. Speaker. This matter should have been dealt with long ago by the minister and the anti-dumping tribunal, but there are some strange happenings and some stange anomalies in the Trudeau administration. The government, figuratively, is not "looking after the store."
The chairman of the anti-dumping tribunal is apparently too busy with his varied commercial activities, trying to sell and introduce the products and munitions of other countries to Canadian consumers. There must be terribly illegal conflict of interest there.
The situation of the textile industry is a case which should be dealt with immediately by the anti-dumping tribunal. What about the cabinet? It does not seem to be interested in the welfare of Canadian industry. Far from it, the ministers are busy now drumming up support for the abolition of capital punishment in the coming vote on Tuesday night, and there is one minister over in France deeply interested in the dangerous proposition of pressing bilingualism into air traffic control in Canada.
You cannot blame me for pointing this out, for most of us here know that if Canadian industry, and especially secondary industry as in this case, does not prosper, then neither does our country nor its workers in industry. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Roy), when speaking during yesterday's textile debate, said that an increased willingness to buy Canadian would be one element in the solution to the problems of the industry. That is all very well, and I think most of us do try to buy Canadian. But we see in our stores a flood of foreign goods from Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Korea where the workers in the plants receive 14 cents an hour, Canadian equivalent. This flood of cheap goods is so great that lately one picks up quite a few garments from display cases in stores before finding one made in Canada.
Having regard to the problems of polyester yarn products in the textile industry, I brought to the attention of the House last week the fact that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce had then had a major recommendation of the Clothing and Textile Board for over five weeks. The hon. member for Laval (Mr. Roy) replied on behalf of the minister that no action would be taken until the end of June. The minister is thus taking seven weeks or more to act in a crisis where action in two weeks was indicated.
I was distressed initially by this reply, having in mind the hardship it implies for the hundreds of people who have been laid off their jobs in Frontenac, Lennox and Addington, and in the Kingston district and other constituencies where this product is efficiently made and processed. Further investigation of the problem has revealed something more distressing still.
Previous outbreaks of the polyester yarn problem were studied on two occasions by the Clothing and Textile Board. The board made recommendations in December, 1972, and in February, 1975. In both cases the government failed to table or implement the recommendation of its board. The present inaction of the government, which the hon. member for Laval says will continue until June 30, when this House rises, suggests that the government may not be taking any action at all to restore the loss of jobs.

In this grave matter affecting hundreds of my constituents, I request that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce tabled without further delay the recommendations made by the Clothing and Textile Board five weeks ago, and to announce immediately the actions the government will take to implement them.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Roy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: INDUSTRY-TEXTILES-REQUEST FOR TABLING OF REPORT OF CLOTHING AND TEXTILE BOARD ON POLYESTER YARN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am somewhat surprised to hear tonight about that matter on the late show on a subject that was debated yesterday during an opposition day. I would have preferred to see the hon. member for Frontenac-Lennox and Addington (Mr. Alkenbrack) participating in the debate we had yesterday. He would have understood what the textile policy was. I think the only answer I would have to give would be the following. Either the hon. member just wants to table a report without it having been considered to determine its full application and implications for all parties involved, or he wants the report to be brought forward without any follow-up, or again perhaps he wants some time to be taken to consider the implications of that report and then see what it could mean for the parties involved.
I would refer the hon. member to the speech made yesterday by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson), as reported at page 14578 of Hansard, and he will see then the exact answer given to his question, and I quote:
I do not, however, deny the legitimacy of the claim that the process is on the slow side. I have looked into this and asked that once a report comes in from the Clothing and Textile Board there should be no delay in taking appropriate action. In this connection I am faced with something of a dilemma. We could table the report quite quickly after it is received from the board, but the policy has been to hold off publication of the report until a decision has been made on the action to be taken.
I suggest that if we table the report without simultaneously announcing our decision on the action to be taken a whole series of representations could be made which would further delay the process. For the moment we think it is preferable to receive the report, decide on the action to be taken, and made the announcement accordingly. If hon. members think that another amendment to that method could further step up things and they have information or know another procedure that could be used we would be quite happy to listen in an objective manner.
So, Mr. Speaker, once again I am somewhat surprised to see that matter discussed on the late show because if the hon. member had participated in the debate yesterday he would have had the answer.

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-REGIONAL PRODUCERS' REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION-GOVERNMENT ACTION
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-REGIONAL PRODUCERS' REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 4 a group of producers representing all the producers within the CBC who are not of the Toronto-based organization put out a news release asking for the establishment of a royal commission to examine the organizational structure of the CBC and to find ways of decentralize that organization. I rose on June 8 to ask the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) the following question:
June 17, 1976

Can the Secretary of State inform the House of any of the substance of the president's discussion and why the producers across Canada had to resort to this public call for a royal commission?
Would you believe, Mr. Speaker, that the minister's answer was as follows:
I myself met with some members of the committee two weeks after his meeting. There is a problem which arises out of the success of our regionalization.
That is a staggering statement. I wish to give a couple of examples of the ludicrous nature of that kind of statement. I have before me a question from the order paper which was put by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds), dated March 25, in which he asked why the ten o'clock p.m. CBC radio news program coming from Vancouver is to be cancelled on April 1, 1977. Here, among some other reasons, is what the CBC representative wrote:
The English services division of the CBC decided that the resources available in the British Columbia region would be better devoted to improving B.C. newscasts and B.C. contributions to national newscasts than to the largely editing job involved in the present 10 p.m. news.
First of all, the answer does not tell you who the English services division is. Obviously it is part of the division in Toronto which cut off the news program coming from Vancouver. It means that all those people in the Koote-nays, in the Chilcotin region, in the north country, in the Okanagan, who want local farm news from Vancouver are not going to get that program any more because Toronto knows best. Toronto will decided what will be on the ten o'clock news. But the English services division in Toronto has decided how those resources should be distributed. That is exactly the argument.
What is bothering the producers and directors across Canada within the CBC? Is is not that they do not have quality equipment; it is that they have no decision making power. Toronto knows best. Because I knew that the president of the CBC was going to Vancouver to meet with this informal group known as the Committee of 100,1 posed the question to him when he appeared before the Broadcasting Committee on May 6. I asked him about the pilot project of the Peter Gzowski show. Somebody told me that a group of 16 technicians had been shipped from Toronto to Vancouver to do that pilot project. Mr. MacPherson, the vice-president and general manager of the CBC English services division, happened to give me the answer at that time. Here is what he said:
The unit would be a producer, researchers, bascially the travelling group that also produced the pilot program, there would be a director involved-
Here we have a program produced and directed in Vancouver, but the CBC has to bring their crew from Toronto to do it in Vancouver and, above all, they bring a research man. What kind of lunacy is it to have researchers coming from Toronto to produce a show in Vancouver?
The Secretary of State has the gall to say that the problem of directors and producers in B.C. stems from the fact that the CBC has been overly successful. We have a $30 million monument in Vancouver which looks like a grain elevator. The government has poured $30 million into that building, but the CBC is keeping the producers and directors there out of work because Toronto wants to make the decisions. Any time there is a program emanating from
Adjournment Debate
Vancouver it looks across the country for producers and directors to put on that show. And what do you know, you cannot find any good ones in Vancouver so you have to bring them from Toronto! The same is true for the Mari times.
I know the parliamentary secretary cannot speak on this subject, but I know Nova Scotia is suffering in this way, and so is New Brunswick and Newfoundland just because Toronto thinks it is God and has all the answers and nobody else in the country knows anything.
A few weeks ago the House passed a resolution unanimously asking the committee to examine why the CBC abandoned or cut back its farm broadcasts. This is another example of CBC in Toronto deciding that there is a segment of the community in Canada that does not need the show that is going on. This is the point of my question to the Secretary of State. Why has he this penchant, this fixation, on buildings and equipment but not on people who produce the show in the first place?
While I think a royal commission is no answer to this because the report would be gathering dust as soon as it was finished, we do need a Secretary of State who will be serious about the real issues in public broadcasting. Forget about all the fancy, sexy projects that he has going in the country, and get to work to provide the kind of projects that will find work for the producers and directors in Canada and bring about unity.
The president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has said that one of the greatest issues within the CBC is that there are a lot of fractious factions within the CBC. The reason is that nothing is being done which will honour the intelligence and the decision-making processes in the regions.

speakeroldname: Miss Coline Campbell (Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-REGIONAL PRODUCERS' REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member emphasizes that it is the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) who is in charge of the CBC, but the CBC comes to the committee quite often, and the hon. member can question there.
During questioning on May 7, 1976, by the hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) when the CBC was before the broadcasting committee, the CBC president, Mr. A. W. Johnson, outlined how he intended to deal with the three major propositions of the Committee of 100. One proposition had to do with the autonomy of decision-making within the British Columbia region; one proposition had to do with the extent of production in the British Columbia region; and the third proposition had to do with the kind of programming that CBC should be emphasizing.
In connection with those propositions, Mr. Johnson told the broadcasting committee meeting that as for the autonomy of decision-making in respect of productions for the network, the CBC must use the best talents, the best executive producers and producers that it can find and that the CBC regards the producers in British Columbia as it regards the producers in Toronto, as being a pool on which to draw. Excellence, not quotas, must be used as the basis for the CBC's determination of what is the best team for producing programming which relates to a particular part of the country.
At the subsequent meeting with the Committee of 100,
Mr. Johnson stressed his concern for proper balance be-

June 17, 1976
Adjournment Debate
tween national, regional and local programming and for over-all consultation in the program decision-making process at all levels. He assured the Committee of 100 that this area would be a priority for regular review during his term of office.
At the meeting in Vancouver the CBC president further agreed, as he had said he would when before the broadcasting committee, to give the Committee of 100 the facts, both in statistical and program terms, on what is being produced regionally for regional consumption, what is being produced and used in other centres across Canada in the regional exchanges, and, thirdly, the amount of production emanating from British Columbia on the national network.
On the third question concerning programming emphasis, Mr. Johnson told the broadcasting committee, and subsequently the Committee of 100 in Vancouver, that he thought the short generalization of the point of view of the Vancouver group was that the CBC should leave situation comedies, family dramas, and variety to the Americans because they are good at them. If the CBC were to do that,
he said, it would be leaving to the Americans a very large proportion of programming and viewing time of Canadians, and he did not believe that would be a good thing.
The desire of CBC television producers for even more regional involvement is understandable and CBC program managers in Toronto and the regions have discussed and will continue to discuss this question with producers.
I am informed further that the CBC has been reviewing over the past several months both its regional organization and regional program production, production both for regional and network use. It was with this review in mind that the CBC president visited all regions of the corporation during his first nine months in office and met with representatives of the Committee of 100 in Vancouver last month. Mr. Johnson has advised that he expects to be in a position to make a statement sometime this fall on the proposals which result from this review.
